Apache HTTP Server

The apache SSL config file differs depending on different platforms:
     Windows
     The apache SSL config file is <APACHE24_HOME>/conf/extra/httpd-ssl.conf , the <APACHE24_HOME> refers to the
     install directory of the Apache HTTP Server.
     You need to load necessary modules and include the httpd-ssl.conf file in
     the <APACHE24_HOME>\conf\httpd.conf file first, for example:

          ...
          LoadModule socache_shmcb_module modules/mod_socache_shmcb.so
          ...
          LoadModule ssl_module modules/mod_ssl.so
          ...
          # Secure (SSL/TLS) connections
          Include conf/extra/httpd-ssl.conf
          ...

     Linux
     The apache SSL config file is <APACHE24_HOME>/conf.d/ssl.conf , the <APACHE24_HOME> refers to
     the /etc/httpd directory.
Copy the smrootca.crt, apache.crt, and apache.key files to the <APACHE24_HOME>/conf/ folder, and then edit the apache
SSL config file as follows.

  <VirtualHost _default_:443>
      SSLEngine on
      ServerName apache.yourdomain.net:443
      SSLCertificateFile "${ServerRoot}/conf/ssl/apache.crt"
      SSLCertificateKeyFile "${ServerRoot}/conf/ssl/apache.key"
      SSLCACertificateFile "${ServerRoot}/conf/ssl/smrootca.crt"
      SSLProxyEngine on
      SSLProxyCACertificateFile "${ServerRoot}/conf/ssl/smrootca.crt"
      ...

  </virtualhost>

Note: The SSLCACertificateFile directive is only needed if you set up the Common Access Card (CAC) sign-on in the web
tier. It needs to be the root CA certificate of your organization in the production environment. In the test and development
environment, you need to use smrootca.crt if the end-users' certificate is issued by the Service Manager private CA.
It's strongly recommended that you set secure TLS protocols and cipher suites in the apache SSL config file. For example:

  SSLProtocol all -TLSv1.1 -TLSv1 -SSLv3
  SSLProxyProtocol all -TLSv1.1 -TLSv1 -SSLv3
  SSLCipherSuite ECDHE:!SHA1
  SSLProxyCipherSuite ECDHE:!SHA1

Note:
     You can use the openssl ciphers -v command to view effective cipher suites of the given cipher-spec string.
     For example:
      Windows:

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 81 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

        <APACHE24_HOME>\bin\openssl ciphers -v "ECDHE:!SHA1"

     Linux:

        openssl ciphers -v 'ECDHE:!SHA1'

     You can also set explicit cipher suites instead of aliases.
     For example:

          SSLCipherSuite TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-
          SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384

Depending on the protocol you want to use between the Apache HTTP Server and Tomcat, you need to add some additional
settings to the apache SSL config file.

     AJP
     Use the ajp:// prefix when defining the URL of the ProxyPass or BalancerMember directive. For example:

          # If the backend is a tomcat cluster
          <Proxy "balancer://webtierCluster">

             BalancerMember "ajp://smwebtier.yourdomain.net:8009" secret=MyT0mcAt route=1.1
          timeout=300

             BalancerMember "ajp://smwebtier.yourdomain.net:8019" secret=MyT0mcAt route=1.2
          timeout=300

             ProxySet lbmethod=bybusyness stickysession=JSESSIONID nofailover=On
          </Proxy>
          ProxyPass /webtier balancer://webtierCluster/webtier

          # If the backend is a single tomcat instance
          ProxyPass /mobility ajp://smmobility.yourdomain.net:8009/mobility secret=MyT0mcAt retry=0

     HTTPS
     Use the https:// prefix when defining the URL of the ProxyPass or BalancerMember directive. For example:

          # If the backend is a tomcat cluster
          <Proxy "balancer://webtierCluster>

             BalancerMember "https://smwebtier.yourdomain.net:8443" route=1.1 timeout=300
             BalancerMember "https://smwebtier.yourdomain.net:8453" route=1.2 timeout=300
             ProxySet lbmethod=bybusyness stickysession=JSESSIONID nofailover=On
          </Proxy>
          ProxyPass /webtier balancer://webtierCluster/webtier
          <Location "/webtier">
             RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host expr=%{HTTP_HOST}
             RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto expr=%{REQUEST_SCHEME}
          </Location>

          # If the backend is a single tomcat instance
          ProxyPass /mobility https://smmobility.yourdomain.net:8443/mobility retry=0

     Note: For the webtier, you need either set the X-Forwarded-* HTTP request headers as above, or set

1.8.12.4. TLS 1.2 support and configuration

When the Service Manager web tier and the Mobility client act as TLS/SSL servers, they use the Oracle or IBM Java virtual
machine (JVM) that's required by your third-party web applications server to securely manage and connect incoming client
requests that use TLS or SSL protocols. Examples of client requests include requests that originate from web browsers that
are running on end-user's workstations. Depending on the third-party web application server, these connections default to
the highest supported version of the TLS/SSL protocol. We don't provide the software that hosts the Service Manager web
tier or Mobility client products; and it is this software that controls the specific TLS/SSL protocols that are used. As such, we
recommend that you consult the vendor of your browser and third-party web application server (such as IBM Websphere and
Apache Tomcat) for information about how to configure TLS 1.2.

As of Service Manager 9.41, the web tier, Mobility client and Windows client use TLS 1.2 by default.

The Service Manager server uses Java to securely manage and connect incoming client requests that use TLS and SSL
protocols. In this scenario, the Service Manager server is acting as a TLS/SSL server. As of Service Manager 9.41, the Service
Manager server uses TLS 1.2 by default. To enforce the TLS 1.2 protocol, configure the following parameter in the sm.ini file:

sslEnabledProtocols:TLSv1.2

            Note

           TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are versions of the TLS protocol that are no longer considered secure and have been disabled by
           default. If you encounter issues, you can, at your own risk, re-enable the versions. See Re-enable the acceptance
           of a Java certificate algorithm for more information.

When the Service Manager server acts as a TLS/SSL client, it uses OpenSSL to connect to the Directory Services server via
the secure LDAP protocol. Secure LDAP is also known as LDAP over SSL (LDAPS). Depending on the Directory Service
server, these connections will default to the highest supported version of the TLS/SSL protocol. To force the Service Manager
server to establish only TLS 1.2 connections with the LDAP server, set the following environment variable in the operating
system:

LDAPTLS_PROTOCOL_MIN=3.3

            Note

           For information about how to set an environment variable, refer to your operating system's documentation or to
           your server administrator.

The Service Manager server may act as a TLS/SSL client to securely connect to SMTP servers or to consume third-party
external Web Services over HTTPS, depending on the SMTP Server or the Web Services server. These connections will
default to TLS 1.2. To enforce the TLS 1.2 protocol for these scenarios, configure the following parameter in the sm.ini file:

sslEnabledProtocols:TLSv1.2

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 87 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

1.8.12.5. TLS 1.3 support and configuration

The TLS/SSL protocol secures the connection between two communication endpoints, typically the client and the server.
OpenText recommends using TLS 1.3 in Service Manager. For web clients, URLs that require a secure connection start with
HTTPS instead of HTTP. You can enable TLS/SSL communications between:

     The browsers and the Service Manager web tier
     The browsers and the Service Manager Mobility client
     The Service Manager web tier and Service Manager server
     The Service Manager Mobility client and Service Manager server
     Service Manager server and optional Directory Services Server (LDAP server)
     Service Manager server and optional Smart Analytics Server (IDOL)
     Service Manager server and third-party Web Services integrations
     Service Manager Smart Email solution and a third-party email server

As of Service Manager 9.80, the Service Manager supports TLS 1.3. To enforce the TLS 1.3 protocol, follow these steps.

1.8.12.6. Re-enable the acceptance of a Java certificate
algorithm

The Service Manager server no longer accepts Java certificates that are generated by using certain "weak" algorithms. If you
used these algorithms to generate your Java certificates, you must now regenerate them by using a more complex algorithm,
such as RSA.

We strongly recommend that you regenerate the Java certificates by using a more complex algorithm. If it's not practical to
do so, you can disable this enhancement. However, disabling this enhancement lowers the security profile of Service
Manager and you're not adhering to the known security best practices.

Follow these steps to disable this enhancement:

   1. Open the extra.java.security file that's located in the RUN folder.
   2. Comment out or delete the contents of the file.
   3. Restart the Service Manager server.

Alternatively, you can re-enable the acceptance of specific algorithms. For more information about the security best
practices for enabling the secure algorithms, refer to https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS. Note that disabling
certain algorithms may cause connectivity issues between Service Manager and third-party web service clients. You may
need to perform thorough connectivity testing after you update this file.

The following algorithms are no longer accepted:

     MD5
     DSA
     3DES_EDE
     DES_CBC
     DHE, RC4
     SSLv3
     TLSv1
     ECDH_anon
     DH_anon
     NULL
     DH keySize < 768
     RSA keySize < 2048

1.8.13. Support of the HTTP Strict Transport Security protocol

HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a web security policy mechanism, which helps protect web application users from
some passive (eavesdropping) and active network attacks. As of Service Manager 9.72, the HSTS response header is
automatically added on the web tier side when the web parameter cookie.secure is set to true . To enable HSTS for Service
Manager Mobility Client, you only need to enable HSTS in the web server or the web application server. Hence, HSTS adds
an HTTP header named Strict-Transport-Security when establishing an HTTPS session.

            Important

                If you are using a web server (Apache or IIS) in front of your web application server (Tomcat), you only need
                to enable HSTS in the web server; otherwise, you need to enable HSTS in the web application server.
                HSTS works only for ports 80 and 443. Make sure you have configured the web server or web application
                server to use port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS.
                To use HSTS, be sure to enable the secureLogin parameter in the Service Manager Mobility Client and
                configure SSL between the web application server and browser.

The following are instructions on how to enable HSTS in the supported web servers and web application servers.

How to enable HSTS in Tomcat

To enable HSTS in Tomcat, follow these steps:

   1. Open the <Tomcat>/conf/web.xml file in a text editor.
   2. Uncomment the httpHeaderSecurity filter definition and the <filter-mapping> section.
   3. Add the hstsMaxAgeSeconds parameter and the antiClickJackingOption parameter as shown below.

          <filter>
                 <filter-name>httpHeaderSecurity</filter-name>
                 <filter-class>org.apache.catalina.filters.HttpHeaderSecurityFilter</filter-class>
                 <init-param>
                     <param-name>hstsMaxAgeSeconds</param-name>
                     <param-value>31536000</param-value>
                 </init-param>
                 <init-param>
                     <param-name>antiClickJackingOption</param-name>
                     <param-value>SAMEORIGIN</param-value>
                 </init-param>
                 <async-supported>true</async-supported>

          </filter>
          ...
          <filter-mapping>

                 <filter-name>httpHeaderSecurity</filter-name>
                 <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern>
                 <dispatcher>REQUEST</dispatcher>
          </filter-mapping>

   4. Save the file.
   5. Restart Tomcat.

How to enable HSTS in Apache

To enable HSTS in an Apache server, follow these steps:

   1. Open the <Apache>/conf/httpd.conf file in a text editor.
   2. Uncomment the header module:

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 91 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

          LoadModule headers_module modules/mod_headers.so

   3. Add a header setting in the VirtualHost section:

          <VirtualHost _default_:80>
          ServerName apache.yourdomain.net:80
          Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubdomains; preload"
          </VirtualHost>

   4. Restart Apache.

How to enable HSTS in IIS

To enable HSTS in IIS, do the following:
   1. Add a Strict-Transport-Security header to the web.config file under the IIS installation root directory:

          <system.webServer>
          <httpProtocol>
          <customHeaders>
          <add name="Strict-Transport-Security" value="max-age=31536000"/>
          </customHeaders>
          </httpProtocol>
          </system.webServer>

   2. Restart IIS.

1.8.14. Enable SSL for PostgreSQL

If your PostgreSQL database requires SSL, you can enable SSL connections between the Service Manager server and the
PostgreSQL database server.
To do this, follow these steps:

Configure PostgreSQL connection in Service Manager server

   1. Prepare the required certification.
     Note: Customized file names and locations of the client certificate, client key, and root certificate are used in this
     example. You can also follow the PostgreSQL SSL documentation to use the default file names and locations.
        1. Prepare the root certificate. For example, if you use self-signed root certification:

                 openssl req -new -nodes -text -out pgroot.csr -keyout pgroot.key -subj
                 "/C=CN/ST=Shanghai/L=Shanghai/O=BTO/CN=root.<your domain name>"
                 openssl x509 -req -in pgroot.csr -text -days 3650 -extensions v3_ca -signkey pgroot.key
                 -out pgroot.crt

           Note: In a production environment, you are recommended to use your own certificate that's signed by your
           corporate CA or a third-party CA.
        2. Prepare the PostgreSQL database server certificate and server private key. For example:

                 openssl req -new -nodes -text -out pgserver.csr -keyout pgserver.key -subj
                 "/C=CN/ST=Shanghai/L=Shanghai/O=BTO/CN=<db server FQDN>"
                 openssl x509 -req -in pgserver.csr -text -days 365 -CA pgroot.crt -CAkey pgroot.key -
                 CAcreateserial -out pgserver.crt

        3. Prepare the client certificate and client private key. For example:

                 openssl req -new -nodes -text -out pgclient.csr -keyout pgclient.key -subj
                 "/C=CN/ST=Shanghai/L=Shanghai/O=BTO/CN=<Postgres DB User Name>"
                 openssl x509 -req -in pgclient.csr -text -days 365 -CA pgroot.crt -CAkey pgroot.key -
                 CAcreateserial -out pgclient.crt

           For details, see the PostgreSQL documentation.
   2. Configure PostgreSQL database files and restart postgreSQL.

        1. Configure pg_hba.conf by appending a line for hostssl. For example:

                 hostssl all all <SM Server FQDN> cert

           Note: If your Service Manager server is configured as horizontal scaling, you need to add each host as an entry in
           the pg_hba.conf file.
        2. Add the root certificate, PostgreSQL server certificate, and PostgreSQL server private key (created in step 1.a and
           step 1.b) to $PGDATA . For example, /var/lib/pgsql/16/data .
        3. Configure postgresql.conf by updating the following parameters:

                 ssl=on
                 ssl_ciphers=<cipher name>
                 ssl_cert_file=<server certificate file name>
                 ssl_key_file=<server private key file name>
                 ssl_ca_file=< root certificate file name>
                 ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.2'
                 ssl_max_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.3'

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 93 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

        4. Restart the PostgreSQL service.
           Note: If you need to configure SSL between Service Manager Collaboration and PostgreSQL, you can restart the
           PostgreSQL service later after the step 8.

   3. Upload the following certificate files to the RUN folder of the Service Manager server.
           Root certificate
           Client certificate
           Client private key

     Notes:
           When Service Manager Server is on Linux, make sure that you set the file permission as 600 for certifications.
           Optionally, you can set Certificate Revocation List (CRL) file.

   4. Add the FQDN of the database server to the host file of the Service Manager server. Alternatively, you can add user
     mapping by following the PostgreSQL document.

          sqldictionary:postgresql
          [postgresql]
          sqldb:host=<dbhost> port=5432 dbname=<dbname> sslmode=verify-full sslcert=pgclient.crt
          sslkey=pgclient.key sslrootcert=pgroot.crt

           sslmode: secure connections can be ensured by setting the parameter to verify-full or verify-ca
           sslcert: specifies the client certificate
           sslkey: specifies the client private key
           sslrootcert: specifies the root certificate
     Tip: For more information, see the PostgreSQL documentation: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-ssl.html

   6. Configure the pgsslEnableProtocols and pgsslEnableCiphers parameters in sm.ini.
           pgsslEnableProtocols: specifies the supported SSL protocols for PostgreSQL SSL connections. TLSv1.2, TLSv1.3
           is set by default. For details, see pgsslEnableProtocols.

           pgsslEnableCiphers: specifies an array of cipher suites used for PostgreSQL SSL connections. For details, see
           pgsslEnableCiphers.

   7. Restart the Service Manager server.

Configure PostgreSQL connection for Chat

   1. If you use Service Manager Collaboration, configure the JDBC client for the Chat server.
        1. Run the following command to convert the private key created in step 1.c from the PEM format to the DER format,
           and then name it to pgclient.pk8 .

                 # openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -outform DER -in pgclient.key -out pgclient.pk8 -
                 nocrypt

        2. Copy certificates to the Chat server.

        4. Add the FQDN of the database server to the host file of the Chat server. Alternatively, you can add user mapping

1.8.15. Trusted sign-on

You can configure Service Manager clients to automatically log on using the same authentication information as users
entered when they logged onto their client workstation's operating system. When you enable trusted sign-on, users bypass
the Service Manager logon screen and directly enter the application.

In a trusted sign-on scenario the Service Manager server grants access to clients only if the following conditions are met.

     The user's logon credentials match an existing operator record in Service Manager or a valid LDAP source that Service
     Manager recognizes.
     A trusted authentication authority, such as the operating system, validates that the user's logon credentials are valid.
     The client (Service Manager Web Tier or Windows) must present a signed SSL certificate.

The following figure depicts the connection process between a Web server, a Web application server, and the Service
Manager application server:

     The Web server receives the user information from the client via the browser, and passes the user name and domain
     name to the Web application server.
     The Web application server (such as Tomcat) acts as a client, and communicates with the Service Manager application
     server.
     The Service Manager application server also checks whether the user was authenticated by a valid domain. Local
     machine authentication is not accepted; if attempted the Service Manager server will reject such a request.

1.8.15.1. Requirements for trusted sign-on

This configuration is intended for customers who have an Service Manager server running in a secured environment and
want users to be able to log on to the server without providing a user name and password.

Parameters required in the server configuration file (sm.ini)

  trustedsignon:1
  ssl:1
  ssl_reqClientAuth:2

Parameters required in the web tier configuration file (web.xml)

isCustomAuthenticationUsed - Set the value to false to make Service Manager send the current user name in the HTTP
header.

Other requirements

   1. Configure the web tier to use a trusted authentication source.
        1. Stop the web application server running the web tier.
        2. Navigate to the folder <web tier installation path>\WEB-INF\classes , and open the file application-context.xml in
           a text editor.
        3. Search for the following string:
            <sec:filter-chain pattern="/**" filters="securityContextPersistenceFilter,resourceFilter,anonymousAuthFilter"/>
        4. Add preAuthenticationFilter to use Microsoft Integrated Windows Authentication as your trusted authentication
           source:
            <sec:filter-
           chain pattern="/**" filters="securityContextPersistenceFilter,resourceFilter,preAuthenticationFilter,anonymousAuth
           Filter"/>
        5. Configure the parameters in the bean definition of preAuthenticationFilter according to the username format used
           in Service Manager.

                 keepDomain:
                 true, the login name of the Service Manager operators contains the domain name;
                 false (default), does not contain.

                 userPrincipalNameFormat:
                 true, User Principal Name (UPN) format - for example: UserName@DOMAIN is used;
                 false (default), Down-Level Logon Name format - for example: DOMAIN\UserName is used.

           In the example above, DOMAIN is the "Domain name (pre-Windows 2000)" of your Active Directory.
        6. Save the file and restart the web application server.
   2. Create an operator record for each Windows user that you want to log on to Service Manager. Format of the username
     must match the configuration in step 1 > e.
   3. Install and configure an external authentication source, such as Microsoft Integrated Windows Authentication, to ensure
     that Service Manager can use your private certificates.
   4. Refer to Example: Configuring the Web server for trusted sign-on to configure a web server for trusted sign-on.
   5. Beginning with Service Manager 9.30, Trusted Sign-On (TSO) requires the use of ssl_reqClientAuth:2 . You must create
     unique client SSL certificates for each Service Manager client that needs to access Service Manager with TSO. For
     example, if you have 20 Windows clients, you must create 20 unique client SSL certificates.

1.8.15.2. Example: Enabling trusted sign-on

Trusted sign-on in Service Manager leverages Windows-integrated authentication that allows users on trusted clients who
have logged in to a Windows domain to log on to Service Manager without providing a user name and password. The
Windows client can directly retrieve the cached credentials from the Windows system to authenticate the operator.
For applications deployed on a Java EE application server, such as web tier and mobility, integration with a web server (such
as Windows Internet Information Services (IIS) or Apache HTTP server) is required for the authentication.

            Note

                Service Manager only supports trusted sign-on with SSL enabled and the ssl_reqClientAuth parameter set
                to "2".
                To use trusted sign-on, you must first add your web server and Windows clients to a domain.

This example assumes that you are using Tomcat as the web application server and Apache or IIS as the web server.
To enable trusted sign-on, perform the following tasks:

Task 1: Create an operator record for each Windows user

You need to create an operator record for each Windows user so that they can log in to Service Manager.
There are two account formats for a Windows user in an Active Directory:

     sAMAccountName format.
     For example, DOMAIN\UserName. Here DOAMIN is the "Domain name (pre-Windows 2000)" of your Active Directory.
     UserPrincipalName format.
     For example, UserName@xxx.com.

Note that when you are using Windows integrated authentication, the account name passed to the web server is different
based on the authentication type.

     For NTLM, the system always retrieves sAMAccountName as the account name even if you have logged on to the
     computer using the UserPrincipalName.
     For GSSAPI, the system returns the account name in the format of UserName@KerberosRealm. Usually the
     KerberosRealm is the same as the domain name.

The default configuration of trusted sign-on is to drop the domain part from the account name. Hence, when you create an
operator in Service Manager, the login name doesn't contain domain name.
Suppose your Service Manager operators are from multiple domains. When you create an operator in Service Manager, the
login name must contain domain name. You can use either the sAMAccountName format or the UserPrincipalName format.
Note that in both formats the domain part is as follows.

     For NTLM, it is from sAMAccountName - the "Domain name (pre-Windows 2000)" of your Active Directory.
     For GSSAPI, it is the KerberosRealm.

Task 2: Enable required SSL encryption and trusted clients.

For detailed steps, see Configure two-way SSL.

Task 3: Configure the web tier to use trusted sign-on.

If the web server connects to Tomcat by using the AJP protocol, please follow below steps:

   1. Stop the web application server running the web tier.
   2. In the web tier's web.xml file, set isCustomAuthenticationUsed to false.
   3. In the <Tomcat>/conf/server.xml file, insert tomcatAuthentication="false" in the following section as shown below.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 99 of 251
                                                                                                                                                           Service Manager 9.81

      <Connector protocol="AJP/1.3"
         secret="MyT0mcAt"
         address="0.0.0.0"
         port="8009"
         tomcatAuthentication="false"
         redirectPort="8443" />

4. Edit the web application server's application-context.xml file to enable pre-authentication.
     1. Open <web tier installation path>\WEB-INF\classes\application-context.xml in a text editor, and search for the
        following string:
         <sec:filter-chain pattern="/**" filters="securityContextPersistenceFilter,resourceFilter,anonymousAuthFilter"/>
     2. Insert preAuthenticationFilter in the string:
         <sec:filter-
        chain pattern="/**" filters="securityContextPersistenceFilter,resourceFilter,preAuthenticationFilter,anonymousAuth
        Filter"/>
        Note: If you need to enable trusted sign-on for your web client users and also enable web tier lightweight single
        sign-on (LW-SSO) for integrations, add lwSsoFilter followed by preAuthenticationFilter , as shown in the
        following:
         <sec:filter-
        chain pattern="/**" filters="securityContextPersistenceFilter,resourceFilter,lwSsoFilter,preAuthenticationFilter,ano
        nymousAuthFilter"/>
        For information about how to enable LW-SSO in the web tier, see Configure LW-SSO in the Service Manager Web
        tier.
     3. Configure the parameters in the bean definition of preAuthenticationFilter according to the username format
        configured in Task 1.

             keepDomain:
             true, the login name of the Service Manager operators contains the domain name;
             false (default), does not contain.

             userPrincipalNameFormat:
             true, UserPrincipalName format;
             false (default), sAMAccountName format.

     4. If the web server connects to Tomcat by using the HTTPS protocol and passes the user name by a specific request
        header (for example, X-Remote-User ), you need to configure the web tier to get the remote user from the
        specific request header. Edit the <WEBTIER>/WEB-INF/classes/application-context.xml file to use the
         HttpHeaderPreAuthenticationFilter instead of the PreAuthenticationFilter for the preAuthenticationFilter bean.
        For example:

             <bean id="preAuthenticationFilter"
             class="com.hp.ov.cwc.security.spring.HttpHeaderPreAuthenticationFilter">

                 <property name="authenticationManager">
                     <ref bean="authenticationManager"/>

                 </property>
                 <property name="defaultRole">

                     <value>ROLE_PRE</value>
                 </property>
                 <property name="usernameHeaderKey">

                     <value>X-Remote-User</value>
                 </property>
             </bean>

   5. Restart the web application server.

   2. Open a client connection, and on the Connection tab select Use Trusted Sign-on.
   3. Make selections to the Keep domain and User Principal Name format checkboxes according to the username format
     set in Task 1.
   4. Click Apply.

1.8.15.2.1. Example: Configuring the Web server for trusted
sign-on

To enable trusted sign-on for web tier clients, you must install and configure a web server (for example, Microsoft Internet
Information Services (IIS) or Apache), which receives the user information from the client through the browser, and passes
the user name and domain name to the web application server.

            Note

           The following steps assume that the web server and web application server configurations are already
           established and that the only necessary changes to the configurations of these servers are those described
           below.

Apache configuration changes

            Note

           In this example, the mod_authn_ntlm module is used for Apache on Windows and the mod_auth_gssapi module is
           used for Apache on Linux.

Windows

   1. Obtain the mod_authn_ntlm module from a binary distribution. For example, from Apache Haus.
   2. Extract the downloaded *.zip file, and then add the mod_authn_ntlm.so file to the <APACHE_HOME>/modules

     directory.
   3. Load the mod_authn_ntlm module in the <APACHE_HOME>/conf/httpd.conf file.

          # Load mod_authn_ntlm module
          LoadModule auth_ntlm_module modules/mod_authn_ntlm.so

   4. Configure the authentication type for the web application (for example, web tier) by adding the following lines to the
     default virtual host.

          <Location "/webtier">
             AuthName "Service Manager Web Client"
             AuthType SSPI
             NTLMAuth On
             NTLMAuthoritative On
             NTLMOfferBasic Off
             NTLMOmitDomain On
             <RequireAll>
                 Require valid-user
                 Require not user "NT-AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS-LOGON"
             </RequireAll>

          </Location>

     Notes:
     If the Apache HTTP Server connects to Tomcat by using the HTTPS protocol, you need to set the user name to a
     specific request header (for example, X-Remote-User ). For example:

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 105 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

          <Location "/webtier">
             ...
             RewriteEngine On
             RewriteCond %{LA-U:REMOTE_USER} (.+)
             RewriteRule .* - [E=RU:%1]
             RequestHeader set X-Remote-User %{RU}e

          </Location>

     Note:
           The name within the Location tag needs to be the path the user enters to open the Service Manager web client
           website. Usually, the name is taken from the *.war file of the web tier.
           On Windows, the default virtual host is <VirtualHost _default_:80> defined in the
            <APACHE_HOME>/conf/extra/httpd-vhosts.conf file or <VirtualHost _default_:443> defined in the
            <APACHE_HOME>/conf/extra/httpd-ssl.conf file, depending on whether you turn on SSL for the Apache HTTP
           Server.

Linux

   1. On a Linux system, install the mod_auth_gssapi module and the mod_session module. For example:

          $ sudo yum install mod_auth_gssapi
          $ sudo yum install mod_session

   2. Create a user account named apache in the Active Directory (AD) and use this account as the Service Principal for the
     Apache HTTP server (httpd).
     Note: The user logon name is the hostname (without the domain part) where the Apache HTTP server is installed. On
     the Account tab, select User password never expires and This account supports kerberos AES 256 bit encryption
     options.

   3. Open a command prompt in the Windows system of the AD and generate the keytab file for the Apache HTTP server
     with the following command.

          > ktpass -princ HTTP/apache.yourdomain.net@YOURDOMAIN.NET -mapuser apache -crypto AES256-
          SHA1 -ptype KRB5_NT_PRINCIPAL -pass +rndPass -out c:/auth_apachehost_kerb.keytab

   4. Configure the Apache HTTP server to use mod_auth_gssapi with the keytab generated.
     Copy the keytab generated in step 3 from the Windows system to /etc/httpd/conf in the Linux system where the
     Apache HTTP server is installed and set appropriate file permission. For example:

          $ sudo chmod 755 /etc/httpd/conf/auth_apachehost_kerb.keytab

          $ sudo klist -e -k /etc/httpd/conf/auth_apachehost_kerb.keytab
          Keytab name: FILE:/etc/httpd/conf/auth_apachehost_kerb.keytab
          KVNO Principal
          ---- --------------------------------------------------------------------------

               6 HTTP/apache.yourdomain.net@YOURDOMAIN.NET (aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96)

   5. Configure the authentication type for the SM web tier by adding the following lines to the default virtual host in
      /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf .

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 106 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

          <Location "/webtier">
                 AuthType GSSAPI
                 AuthName "Service Manager Web Client"
                 GssapiCredStore keytab:/etc/httpd/conf/auth_apachehost_kerb.keytab
                 GssapiUseSessions On
                 Session On
                 SessionCookieName gssapi_session path=/webtier;httponly;secure;
                 Require valid-user

          </Location>

     Notes:
     If the Apache HTTP Server connects to Tomcat by using the HTTPS protocol, you need to set the user name to a
     specific request header (for example, X-Remote-User ). For example:

          <Location "/webtier">
             ...
             RewriteEngine On
             RewriteCond %{LA-U:REMOTE_USER} (.+)
             RewriteRule .* - [E=RU:%1]
             RequestHeader set X-Remote-User %{RU}e

          </Location>

   6. Check the configuration and restart the Apache HTTP server.

          $ sudo apachectl configtest
          Syntax OK
          $ sudo systemctl restart httpd

IIS configuration changes

            Note

           You need to use either the BonCode AJP 1.3 connector or the Apache JK connector for TSO.

   1. Open the Internet Information Services (IIS) Manager.
   2. Select Default Web Site, and then double-click Authentication. Disable Anonymous Authentication, and then enable

     Windows Authentication. Edit the providers of the Windows Authentication by moving NTLM to the top of the enabled
     providers.

to enable trusted sign-on for web clients.

1.8.15.2.2. Example: Configuring Single Sign-on with third
party authentication on the web tier

Configuring the Web Client for third-party authentication

   1. To activate single sign-on in Service Manager’s web tier, navigate to the <path to Web application>/WEB-INF/classes/
     directory.

   2. Open the application-context.xml file with a text editor. Update
      /**=httpSessionContextIntegrationFilter,anonymousProcessingFilter to
      /**=httpSessionContextIntegrationFilter,preAuthenticationFilter, anonymousProcessingFilter as described in the
     comment in the application-context.xml file.

   3. Save your changes and restart the web server on the Service Manager web tier.
   4. When using IIS you need to configure an ISAPI connector for your Web application server, and you need to modify the

     virtual directory to use Integrated Windows Authentication.

See the Customer Support Web site for Knowledge Base articles about configuring Integrated Windows Authentication on
common Web application servers or refer to Example: Configuring the Web server for trusted sign-on.

Defining a JavaBean® to handle authentication

All modifications for the single or trusted sign-on settings in the Service Manager Web Tier are done in the <path to web
application>/WEB-INF/classes directory in the application-context.xml file.

For Windows-based authentication, out-of-box Service Manager ships with a JavaBean called preAuthenticationFilter, which
is defined as follows:

  <bean id="preAuthenticationFilter"
  class="com.hp.ov.cwc.security.spring.PreAuthenticationFilter">
  <property name="authenticationManager">

      <ref bean="authenticationManager"/>
  </property>
  <property name="defaultRole">

      <value>ROLE_PRE</value>
  </property>
  </bean>

To use another authentication source that passes the username in the HTTP header, you add or replace the
preAuthenticationFilter block with code such as the following.

The following example shows how to add a new filter. To replace the filter, set the bean ID to preAuthenticationFilter (rather
than SiteminderPreAuthenticationFilter as shown below).

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 109 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

  <bean id="SingleSignOnpreAuthenticationFilter"
  class="com.hp.ov.cwc.security.spring.SiteminderPreAuthenticationFilter">
  <property name="authenticationManager">

      <ref bean="authenticationManager"/>
  </property>
  <property name="defaultRole">

      <value>ROLE_PRE</value>
  </property>
  <property name="keepDomain">

      <value>true</value>
  </property>
  <property name="siteminderUsernameHeaderKey">

      <value>USERNAME</value>
  </property>
  <property name="siteminderPasswordHeaderKey">

      <value>PASSWORD</value>
  </property>
  </bean>

In this definition, the siteminderUsernameHeaderKey property passes the user name value from the single sign-on tool to
Service Manager. To successfully pass the user name value, set the <value> element to the name of the property in the
HTTP header that stores the user name in the third-party authentication tool's configuration.
If the HTTP header is as follows, replace <USERNAME> with REMOTE_USER .

  POST /sc61server/ws HTTP/1.1
  Content-Type: text/xml; charset=utf-8
  SOAPAction: "Retrieve"
  Content-Length: 1474
  Expect: 100-continue
  […]
  REMOTE_USER: falcon
  Cookie: $Version=1; SessionId=127.0.0.1:4819

To activate the sign-on filters, modify the following line in the application-context.xml file.

  /**=httpSessionContextIntegrationFilter,
  SingleSignOnpreAuthenticationFilter,preAuthenticationFilter, anonymousProcessingFilter

The SingleSignOnpreAuthenticationFilter has to match the bean ID from above. If you want multiple sign-on filters, add them
in order to the filter chain. If you do this, the first to succeed will provide the authenticated username.
Note: The httpSessionContextIntegrationFilter always needs to be in the first position within the chain.

Integrating Custom Java Classes into the Java Bean

In Service Manager, it is possible to develop and use a custom Java class for third party authentication as well. You can either
write a new custom Java class or modify the existing Java class to fit the new requirements for Service Manager. The
requirements for the new Java class are described in the example of integrating an old Java class into the Service Manager
system. The modified Java class then needs to be put into the web-inf/classes directory, or as a jar file into web-inf/lib.
In the <path to web application>/WEB-INF/classes directory in the application-context.xml file, your bean will then look as
follows:

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 110 of 251
                                                            Service Manager 9.81

<bean id="preAuthenticationFilter"
class="com.hp.ov.cwc.security.spring.<custom java class>">
<property name="authenticationManager">

   <ref bean="authenticationManager"/>
</property>
<property name="defaultRole">

   <value>ROLE_PRE</value>
</property>
</bean>

The main modification you have to do to the old Java code is to remove all mention of the user object, which is not passed
into the class in Service Manager any longer. Instead, we return the user name, if authentication succeeded, or return null if it
failed. This username has to be returned after a successful run of the class.

Example: Creating a custom Java Class for Single-Sign-On using LDAP

This is an example of how to create a custom Java class for Single Sign-On using LDAP authentication. Actual implementation
will vary from system to system, depending on the LDAP server, setup and configuration.

The following classes are required to compile this example:

Class jar file                            Comments
jasypt-1.9.2.jar                          Part of the jasypt package. Copy the jar to <web-inf>\lib

String myUPNuser = "";

{
   try {
       Hashtable env = new Hashtable();
       String adminName = ldapBindDn;
       String adminPassword = ldapBindPassword;
       String ldapURL = ldapServerURL;
       env.put(Context.INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY, "com.sun.jndi.ldap. LdapCtxFactory");

             //set security credentials, note using simple cleartext authentication
             env.put(Context.SECURITY_AUTHENTICATION, "simple");
             env.put(Context.SECURITY_PRINCIPAL, adminName);
             //decrypt the password if it starts with *** else it is clear text, use as is.
             if (adminPassword.indexOf("***") == 0) {

                 adminPassword = adminPassword.substring(3);
                 BasicTextEncryptor textEncryptor = new BasicTextEncryptor();
                 // this password the same as that used to encrypt the adminpassword with FilterEncrypt
                 textEncryptor.setPassword("PssWrd");
                 adminPassword = textEncryptor.decrypt(adminPassword);
             }
             env.put(Context.SECURITY_CREDENTIALS, adminPassword);
             //connect to my domain controller
             env.put(Context.PROVIDER_URL, ldapURL);
             //Create the initial directory context
             LdapContext ctx = new InitialLdapContext(env, null);
             //Create the search controls
             SearchControls userSearchCtls = new SearchControls();
             //Specify the search scope
             userSearchCtls.setSearchScope(SearchControls.SUBTREE_SCOPE);
             //specify the LDAP search filter to find the user in question
             String userSearchFilter = "(&(objectClass=user)(sAMAccountName=" + samUserName + "))";
             //Specify the Base for the search
             String userSearchBase = ldapBaseDn;
             //Specify the attributes to return
             String userReturnedAtts[] = {"userPrincipalName"};
             userSearchCtls.setReturningAttributes(userReturnedAtts);
             //Search for objects using the filter
             NamingEnumeration userAnswer = ctx.search(userSearchBase, userSearchFilter,
  userSearchCtls);
             //Loop through the search results
             while (userAnswer.hasMoreElements()) {
                 SearchResult sr = (SearchResult) userAnswer.next();
                 Attributes attrs = sr.getAttributes();
                 if (attrs != null) {

                    myUPNuser = attrs.get("userPrincipalName").get().toString();
                 }
             }
         } catch (Exception e) {
             System.err.println("Problem searching directory: " + e);
             System.out.println("Problem searching directory: " + e);
         }
         return myUPNuser;
      }

1.8.16. Common Access Card (CAC) sign-on

Starting with version 9.32, the Service Manager web client supports CAC sign-on. System Administrators can configure the
Service Manager server and web client to automatically log on using CAC authentication. CAC sign-on enables users to log in
to the web client directly with a smart card that stores a valid user certificate, and users only need to enter a card PIN,
instead of a user name and password.

            Note

           The Service Manager Windows client doesn't support CAC sign-on.

Supported smart cards

During CAC sign-on, the Service Manager web tier gets access to the user authentication public certificate and its
counterpart private key through the underlying client crypto architecture. In other words, Service Manager doesn't directly
communicate with the card reader. Technically, Service Manager supports any smart cards that store an X.509 user
authentication certificate and are designed to work with smart card middleware (such as ActivClient) that is installed on the
user's computer. The term "Common Access Card (CAC)" in its origin refers to the Unites States Department of Defense
(DoD) issued cards; however, in the Service Manager documentation the term CAC is used in a broader scope and refers to
any of the supported smart cards. Two examples of such smart cards are the Common Access Card issued by DoD and
Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards issued by other US Government agencies.

CAC authentication

A CAC smart card enables two-factor authentication: the CARD being something you have, and the CAC PIN being something
you know. The CAC stores, in a secure way, the card holder's public certificates and its corresponding private keys. One of
those stored certificates with its private keys is used for user authentication. Service Manager uses SSL and CAC
authentication, which utilizes the certificate in the CAC card to identify the CAC card holder details and leverages the built-in
SSL user authentication abilities to ensure that the CAC owner possess the private key. The certificate key-pair proves that
this person is who the person claims to be. For example, if the certificate claims the public key is owned by userX and it was
signed by a Certificate Authority (CA), when the certificate is presented assuming Service Manager trusts the CA (which
means the CA public key is put in Service Manager's trusted CA store), Service Manager would trust the information and then
challenge the person presenting the certificate to prove the person owns the matching private key. If the person provides the
proper PIN, that private key is unlocked and then Service Manager authenticates the client as the one detailed in the
certificate.

Flexible mapping between distinguished name and login name

During CAC sign-on, a unique attribute in the user's certificate is retrieved as the user's Distinguished Name (DN) and sent to
the SM server as the user's login name.

Different organizations may have different definitions for the same attribute in the user's certificate. For example, your
organization may use employee ID for Subject.CN, while another may use user's full name for it. In addition, it is also possible
that an organization needs to use an Subject Alternative Name (SAN) sub-attribute as DN. For this reason, the Service
Manager web tier provides a configuration file ( <web tier installation path>\WEB-INF\classes\cacconf.properties ), which
contains two parameters (certificateFieldExtractDN and certificateOIDMapping) to allow flexible mapping between DN and
login name. For more information, see Example: enabling CAC sign-on.

Required configurations

CAC sign-on requires the following configurations:

     Both of the Service Manager server and web client have been configured to support CAC sign-on mode.

     Two-way SSL is configured between the web server (or the web application server if no web server) and browser.

     Two-way SSL is configured between the Service Manager server and all clients (the web and Windows clients, and web
     services clients such as Mobility, and other integrated products).

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 116 of 251
                                        Service Manager 9.81

Note

Enabling CAC sign-on on the SM server side will affect all SM clients - all SM clients can only connect to the
server through two-way SSL.

     JDK 1.6 or above is installed on the host machine running the web tier.

Compatibility with other sign-on modes

The following table describes whether or not users can use other sign-on modes when CAC sign-on is enabled in the SM
server and web client.

Mode                                    Description
Basic Authentication
                                        Web client: Users can no longer log in to the web client by
                                        entering a user name and password (that is, using basic
                                        authentication). It is impossible that some web client users
                                        use CAC sign-on while some others use basic
                                        authentication. All users must use CAC sign-on.

                                        Windows client: Users can log in to the Windows client
                                        only with basic authentication, but two-way SSL
                                        authentication is required between the server and
                                        Windows client.

Trusted Sign-On (TSO)                   When both CAC sign-on and TSO are configured in the
Lightweight Single Sign-On (LW-SSO)     same web tier, CAC sign-on takes precedence. For this
                                        reason, don't enable CAC sign-on and TSO in the same
                                        web tier at the same time.

                                        The following discussion assumes a scenario where
                                        Product A (which doesn't support CAC access) is
                                        integrated with Service Manager and LW-SSO are enabled
                                        on both product sides.

                                        Outgoing LW-SSO: SM web client users can directly
                                        access product A through LW-SSO. In other words,
                                        outgoing LW-SSO from the web tier works well.

                                        Incoming LW-SSO: Incoming LW-SSO is ignored, and
                                        users can only access SM from product A with a CAC.

Conditions for CAC access

In a CAC sign-on scenario, the Service Manager server grants access to web clients only if the following conditions are met:

     The web browser from the client side sends the user certificate to the web server, and then the web server passes the
     certificate to the web application server.
     The user certificate passes the validation by the web tier.
     The user's logon credentials match an existing operator record in Service Manager or a valid LDAP source that Service
     Manager recognizes.
     The web client presents a signed SSL certificate.

                   Note

                Each Windows client must also present a signed SSL certificate to the server.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 117 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

CAC connection process

The following figure depicts the connection process between a web server, a web application server, and the Service
Manager server in a CAC sign-on scenario.

The following describes how the process works:

   1. The user inserts a CAC into a card reader.
   2. The smart card middleware (such as ActivClient) automatically loads the user's personal certificate ("user certificate")

     from the CAC to the browser.
   3. The browser prompts the user to select an installed certificate to log in.
   4. The user selects the user certificate to log in.
   5. The browser prompts the user to enter the PIN of the user's CAC.
   6. The user enters the correct PIN.
   7. The web server passes the user certificate to the web application server for validation based on a pre-configured

     validation strategy, which can include any combinations of the following checks except that at least one of the following
     options must be included: using a local CRL, using an online CRL, and using the OCSP.

          • Check if the issuer is from a trusted CA (Certificate Authority)
          • Check if the certificate is revoked using a local Certificate Revocation List (CRL)
          • Check if the certificate is revoked using an online CRL
          • Check if the certificate is revoked using the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
          • Check if the certificate has expired
          • Check if the certificate type is Smart Card
   8. The web application server extracts the Distinguished Name (DN) from the user certificate and sends the DN as the
     user's user name to the Service Manager server.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 118 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

   9. The server verifies the DN against the name field in the operator table (when LDAP is not configured) or against the
     LDAP attribute mapped to this field (if LDAP is configured). If the DN value matches an operator name, the server logs
     the user in; otherwise the server rejects the login request.

1.8.16.1. Requirements for CAC sign-on

This configuration is intended for customers who have an Service Manager server running in a secured environment and
want users to be able to log on to the server using a Common Access Card (CAC), without the need to enter a user name and
password.

Parameters required in sm.ini

Service Manager 9.32 or later supports CAC sign-on with two-way SSL enabled and you must set the value of the
ssl_reqClientAuth parameter to 2.
The server parameters required for CAC sign-on are listed as follows.

  cacsignon:1

  ssl:1
  sslConnector:1
  ssl_reqClientAuth:2
  keystoreFile:<servercert.keystore>
  keystorePass:<keystoreFile password>
  truststoreFile:cacerts
  truststorePass:<truststoreFile password>
  ssl_trustedClientsJKS:<trustedclients.jks>
  ssl_trustedClientsPwd:<ssl_trustedClientsJKS password>

Parameters required in web.xml

The following parameters are required in the web tier configuration file ( web.xml ):

      isCustomAuthenticationUsed=false
     Set the value to false to make Service Manager send the current user name in the HTTP header.
      CACLogin=true
     Set the value to true to enable the CAC logon mode in the web tier.

Other requirements

     Configure your web application server to enable CAC authentication. You do so by updating the web tier's application-
     context.xml file. For details, see Example: enabling CAC sign-on.
     When CAC logon is enabled in the server, you can set ssl_reqClientAuth:2 in the sm.ini file. You must then create
     unique client SSL certificates for each Service Manager client wanting to access Service Manager with CAC. For
     example, if you have 20 Service Manager Windows clients, you must create 20 unique client SSL certificates. If you
     have 4 Service Manager Web Tier servers, you must create 4 unique client SSL certificates for them. In addition, you
     need to configure SSL in the web tier configuration file ( web.xml ) and also in the Windows client Preferences setting.
     For details, see Configure two-way SSL.

                   Tip

                If maintaining these unique client SSL certificates incurs unsustainable IT operation costs, you can consider
                the use of the acceptsharedcert:1 parameter, which enables all clients to use a "shared certificate". For
                more information, see Parameter: acceptsharedcert

     CAC sign-on requires two-way SSL connections between the web server (or web application server if no web server)
     and the user's browser. You need to set up two-way SSL on the web server, or on the web application server (if you
     have no web server deployed).
     Each CAC user must have an operator record created in Service Manager.

1.8.16.2. Example: enabling CAC sign-on

This example assumes that you are using Tomcat as your web application server and Apache as your web server.

Prerequisites

Before you proceed, make sure you have met the following prerequisites:

     Your organization has already a Common Access Card (CAC) security system in place; each Service Manager user
     owns a CAC card that stores the user's personal certificate ("user certificate") and you have downloaded your
     organization's CAC root CA certificate.

     Your CAC root CA certificate refers to the root CA certificate that signs the user certificates stored in the CACs. Later,
     you will need to:

           copy it to your web tier host and specify its location in the RootCertPath parameter. See Task 3: Configure the
           web tier to use CAC sign-on.
           let users import it to their web browser. See Task 7: Configure web browsers to enable web client users to use
           CAC.
     You have Keytool and OpenSSL installed on a machine on which you will generate SSL certificates.
     You have configured the web server and the web application server to use SSL. CAC sign-on requires two-way SSL
     authentication between the web server/web application server and the user's browser.For more information on
     configuring two-way SSL on your web server (Apache or IIS), see Configure two-way SSL.

Configuration Tasks

To enable CAC sign-on in your Service Manager system, complete the following tasks.

Task 1: Enable required SSL encryption and trusted clients.

Enable required SSL encryption between the SM server and Windows and web clients. For details, see Configure two-way
SSL.

When the configuration is complete, verify that you can log in to the web client as usual and log in to Windows client with SSL
encryption.

Task 2: Enable CAC sign-on in the SM server.

Set required parameters in the server configuration file ( sm.ini ). For details, see Requirements for CAC sign-on.

Task 3: Configure the web tier to use CAC sign-on.

   1. Stop the web application server running the web tier.
   2. Copy your CAC root certificate (s) to a directory on your web tier host. For example: <webtier>/WEB-INF/

   3. Set the following parameter values in the web tier's web.xml file.

Parameter                               Value
isCustomAuthenticationUsed              false
CACLogin                                true

4. Configure your web application server to use CAC as the trusted authentication source.
     1. Navigate to the <web tier installation direcotry>\WEB-INF\classes folder, and open the application-context.xml
        file in a text editor.

     2. Search for the following string:

         <sec:filter-chain pattern="/**" filters="securityContextPersistenceFilter,anonymousAuthFilter"/>

     3. Replace the search string with the following text to use CAC authentication as your trusted authentication source:

         <sec:filter-chain pattern="/**" filters="securityContextPersistenceFilter,cacFilter,

anonymousAuthFilter"/>

              Paramter: certificateFieldExtractDN
              Default: Subject.CN
              Description:
              This parameter specifies a unique attribute in the user certificate that the web application server extracts as a
              Distinguished Name (DN) and sends to the SM server as the user's user name.
              You can specify a Subject attribute in this parameter. By default, the Subject CN attribute (the certificate
              owner's Common Name) is extracted as the user's DN.
              You can also specify this parameter as one of the following Subject Alternative Name (SAN) sub-attributes:
              RFC822 Name, and Other Name (see the figure below).

     If using a sub-attribute of Other Name, specify the parameter in this format: SAN_OTHERNAME.
     <Alias> , where <Alias> is a name that you specify for the sub-attribute. The user certificate's SAN
     Other Name value that binds to the OID will be extracted as the DN. For example, if you use Other
     Name's Principal Name sub-attribute (also known as UPN, which should be mapped to OID
     "1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.3"), you can specify the following value (where PrincipalName is an alias for Principal
     Name):
      certificateFieldExtractDN=SAN_OTHERNAME.PrincipalName

                   Tip

                As a best practice, avoid including white spaces in alias names. For example, for Principal
                Name, specify PrincipalName or PN as an alias.

                   Note

                Next, you will specify a mapping between the alias and object ID (OID) of the specified sub-
                attribute of SAN Other Name, by using the certificateOIDMapping parameter.

     If using the RFC822 Name sub-attribute, specify the following value:
      certificateFieldExtractDN=SAN.RFC822
Examples:

  certificateFieldExtractDN=Subject.E
  certificateFieldExtractDN=SAN_OTHERNAME.PrincipalName

Paramter: certificateOIDMapping
Default: (empty)
Description:
This parameter specifies a mapping between the <Alias> you specified in certificateFieldExtractDN and an
OID. Specify the parameter in this format: <Alias>:<OID> .
For example, for SAN's Principal Name, specify this mapping:

  certificateOIDMapping=PrincipalName:1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.3

Paramter: validationStrategy
Default: (empty)
Description:

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 124 of 251
                                                                                                                                      Service Manager 9.81

This parameter specifies how the web application server verifies each user certificate.
You can specify a combination of the following values, each of which represents a checking method:

      1 : Check the revocation status of the user certificate using a local Certificate Revocation List (CRL).
      2 : Check the revocation status of the user certificate using an online CRL.
      3 : Check the revocation status of the user certificate using the Online Certificate Status Protocol
     (OCSP).
      4 : Check if the user certificate is of the Smart Card type.
Pay attention to the following:
     You can't leave this parameter empty.
     If you specify more than one value, separate them with a comma. In this case, all specified checking
     methods are used in the sequence they are listed in the parameter.
     You must specify at least one of the following values: 1, 2, and 3. If you don't do so, users will not be
     able to log in; instead, they will see a message in their browser that states "An error has occurred"; in
     the meantime, an error message will occur in the web application server's sm.log file.
     Smart Card checking (value 4) is mandatory for CACs, because CACs are smart cards.
     You can configure CRL or OCSP checking either in your web server or in this parameter, but not in both.
Example:

  validationStrategy=3,4

Parameter: RootCertPath
Default: (empty)
Description:
This parameter specifies the file path (either absolute or relative) to the issuer's CA certificate.

            Note

           The issuer's CA certificate refers to the root CA certificate that signs the user certificates stored
           in the CACs (also referred to as the "CAC root CA certificate" in this document). If you need to
           specify multiple CAC root CA certificates, use a comma to separate them.

Example:

  RootCertPath=/WEB-INF/HPCAB.cer,/WEB-INF/HPCA.cer

Parameter: CRLDownloadURL
Default: (empty)
Description:
Specifies the URL that identifies the location of your online certificate revocation list (CRL).
You can leave this parameter empty, and then the CRL Distribution Point from the user certificate being
validated is retrieved at runtime, which might cause a slightly slower performance; however, if FIPS mode is
enabled in the web client (see FIPS mode), you must explicitly specify this parameter (can't leave it empty).
If your root CA has multi-level intermediate CAs:
If your root CA certificate specified in RootCertPath has multi-level intermediate CA certificates, you should
either specify the multi-level CRLs of the root CA and intermediate CA certificates (comma-separated), or
leave the parameter empty.
Examples:

             CRLDownloadURL=http://onsitecrl.example.com/LatestCRL.crl
             CRLDownloadURL=http://onsitecrl.example.com/LatestCRL.crl,http://onsitecrl.example.
             com/IntermediateCRL.crl

        Parameter: OCSPResponderURL
        Default: (empty)
        Description:
        Specifies the URL that identifies the location of the OCSP responder. By default, this parameter is not
        specified, and the OCSP responder location is retrieved from the user certificate being validated.
        If you specify multiple root CA certificates:
        If you specify multiple root CA certificates in RootCertPath , you must leave OCSPResponderURL empty. In
        this case, the OCSP Responder URL stored in the user certificate being validated is retrieved instead during

        Specifies the location of your local CRL.

Task 4: Configure each Windows client to use SSL.

When CAC sign-on is enabled for the server and web client, the Windows client must run in SSL mode.
Do the following for each Windows client:

  1. Make sure that you have already configured SSL connection between the server and the Windows client. See Task 1:
     Enable required SSL encryption and trusted clients.

   2. Open a client connection.
   3. On the Advanced tab, select Use SSL Encryption, and click Apply.

Task 5: Connect your web application server to the web server.

First, connect Tomcat to Apache. Refer to Configure a web server to redirect requests to the web tier for detailed instructions.
Next, configure the web server and the web application server to use SSL. CAC sign-on requires two-way SSL authentication
between the web server/web application server and the user's browser. For more information on configuring two-way SSL on
your web server (Apache or IIS), see Configure two-way SSL.
If the Apache HTTP Server connects to Tomcat by using the AJP protocol, you need to configure the Apache HTTP Server to
require the client to present a valid certificate. For example, add the following additional settings to the
<APACHE24_HOME>/conf/extra/httpd-ahssl.conf file.

  <Location "/webtier">
      SSLVerifyClient require

  </Location>

If the Apache HTTP Server connects to Tomcat by using the HTTPS protocol, you need to configure the Apache HTTP Server
to require the client to present a valid certificate and configure the Apache HTTP Server to forward the client certificate to the
backend Tomcat through the SSL_CLIENT_CERT request header. For example, add the following additional settings to the
<APACHE24_HOME>/conf/extra/httpd-ahssl.conf file.

<Location "/webtier">
   SSLVerifyClient require
   SSLOptions +ExportCertData
   RequestHeader set SSL_CLIENT_CERT "%{SSL_CLIENT_CERT}s"
   ...

</Location>

Note: Make sure the mod_headers modules are loaded in the <APACHE24_HOME>/conf/httpd.conf file.

1.8.17. Configure IdM authentication in Service Manager

To integrate with the IdM service, you must have an IdM service available.

     In the classic mode (a standalone Service Manager system without integrating with the SMA Service Portal), install a
     standalone IdM service first. For detailed instructions, see Install Identity Manager (IdM).
     In the mixed mode (SMA-SM, a Service Manager system that integrates with the SMA Service Portal), you don't need to
     install the standalone IdM service. Instead, leverage the IdM service deployed in the SMA suite and then integrate
     Service Manager with the IdM service.

Typically, you will deploy a reverse proxy (Apache HTTP Server or IIS) or a hardware load balancer on top of the IdM service
in the production environment. This section uses the Apache HTTP Server as an example for the reverse proxy and assumes
the reverse proxy URL is https://apache.yourdomain.net. The later tasks use this sample reverse proxy URL and you need to
replace it with the actual URL in your environment.

Compatibility with legacy LW-SSO

The IdM authentication is compatible with the legacy LW-SSO solution. If the IdM authentication is enabled in Service
Manager, and another legacy application has legacy LW-SSO enabled, users can access either product from the other
product without the need to enter a user name and password.

            Caution

                The IdM service generates a LWSSO_COOKIE_KEY cookie and can also authenticate a user using tokens in
                the cookie, which makes it compatible with the legacy LW-SSO solution. As a result of this, other web
                applications that have legacy LW-SSO enabled can still get integrated by using LW-SSO. Note that the web
                tier doesn't renew the LW-SSO cookie now when the IdM authentication is enabled. If you want to support
                LW-SSO compatibility with other products, you need to set the expiration period of the LW-SSO token to a
                long time in the global settings of the IdM admin console (for example, 480 minutes).
                The Service Manager Server can have both IdM authentication and LW-SSO enabled if needed. This allows
                other applications of the company to access the SM Server through LW-SSO when necessary.
                If both LW-SSO and the IdM authentication are enabled in the Service Manager server, you only need to
                enable the IdM authentication in the Service Manager web tier or Mobility client. Do not enable LW-SSO in
                these clients at the same time.

            Note

           The LW-SSO compatibility has the following limitations.

                For backend integration, legacy applications using legacy LW-SSO must share an LDAP server with Service
                Manager. Otherwise, you need to synchronize users between legacy applications and Service Manager by
                using external tools. Legacy applications may use a dedicated integration user to log in to Service Manager,
                and you can either add the integration user to the LDAP directory service or add the user to Service
                Manager directly.
                For UI-based SSO, legacy applications using legacy LW-SSO and Service Manager (server, web tier, and
                Mobility) must be in the same domain as the IdM service. This is because the IdM service needs to read the
                LW-SSO cookie written by the applications. Legacy applications and the IdP must share an LDAP server, or
                you need to synchronize users between legacy applications and the IdP by using external tools. Depending
                on the authentication type you configured in the IdM service, the IdP can be the IdM service itself for the DB
                authentication or the LDAP authentication, or ADFS for SAML-based SSO, or Keycloak for OIDC-based SSO.

1.8.17.1. Configure IdM authentication in the Service Manager
Server

To enable IdM authentication in the Service Manager Server, stop the Service Manager server and then add the IdM-related
parameters to the <SM_SERVER>/RUN/sm.ini file as follows.
If you set Signature Algorithm as HS256 in IdM administration console:

  idmssoenabled:1
  idmtenant:SM
  idmsigningkey:<your IdM signing key>

If you set Signature Algorithm as RS256 in IdM administration console:

  idmssoenabled:1
  idmtenant:SM
  idmendpoint:https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service
  idmhttpuser:idmTransportUser
  idmhttppassword:<your password of idmTransportUser>
  idmssltrustall:0
  idmtruststore:smrootca.p12
  idmtruststorepassword:<your password of smrootca.p12>
  idmtruststoretype:pkcs12

            Note

                For more details about the IdM-related parameters, see IdM parameters for the Service Manager server.
                For more information about how to set the appropriate values for common IdM parameters, see How to get
                IdM-related settings.

Next, set up user synchronization by using either IdM or LDAP.

            Caution

                Don't set up user synchronization from both IdM and LDAP. Otherwise, performance issues may occur
                during user login.
                If you configured SAML-based Single Sign-On and selected User-Principal-Name (instead of SAM-
                Account-Name documented in step 10.b of Create a trusted relying party in ADFS) as LDAP Attribute, you
                need to do the following:
                - Synchronize users from LDAP.
                - Set the ldapquerymapping:samAccountName=userPrincipalName parameter in sm.ini. See Startup
                parameter: ldapquerymapping for details.
                - Make sure that the user.principal.name field of operator is mapped to userPrincipalName when you
                Define file and field-level mappings to an LDAP server.

Synchronize users from IdM

Add IdM parameters

You need to add additional IdM parameters to connect to the IdM service. For example:

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 133 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

  idmsyncuser:1
  idmendpoint:https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service
  idmhttpuser:idmTransportUser
  idmhttppassword:<your password of idmTransportUser>
  idmssltrustall:0
  idmtruststore:smrootca.p12
  idmtruststorepassword:<your password of smrootca.p12>
  idmtruststoretype:pkcs12

Now start the Service Manager server and log on to the Windows client to perform the next tasks.

Create operator template

You need to create an operator template named "Template_IdM", which will be applied to the newly synced users.
See Create an operator template for detailed instructions.

            Note

                If you don't create the Template_IdM template, the newly synced users will be assigned with the self-service
                user role.
                The name of the operator template must be set as "Template_IdM".
                The "Template_IdM" template is not applicable for the existing users.
                See Create an operator record from a operator template for more information.

Configure attribute mapping

You need to define how to synchronize the IdM user attributes to Service Manager by configuring attribute mapping. Service
Manager provides the out-of-box mappings for some basic IdM user attributes. You can customize the attribute mappings
except the contact.name field.

   1. From the System Navigator, click System Administration > Ongoing Maintenance > System > IdM Mapping.
   2. The mappings for Operator table and Contact table are displayed.
   3. You may click on an existing attribute mapping to update the value, or add new mappings as required.
   4. Save the changes.

            Important

           Here is the priority order of the IdM mapping, the Template_IdM template, and the existing user attributes:
           IdM mapping > existing user attributes > Template_IdM template
           This means the IdM attributes mapped to Service Manager can overwrite the values defined in the Template_IdM
           template and the existing user attributes. Hence, you need to be careful when configuring the attribute mappings.

1.8.17.2. Configure IdM authentication in the Service Manager
web tier

To enable Identity Manager (IdM) authentication in the web tier, you need to edit the <customize-
folder>/config/webtier.properties file if you have configured the customize-folder parameter, or edit the <WEBTIER>/WEB-
INF/webtier.properties if you haven't configured the customize-folder parameter. Add IdM related settings and set the
isCustomAuthenticationUsed parameter to false . For more information, see IdM parameters for the Service Manager web
tier and mobility client.
See the following configuration as an example:

  idm.sso.enabled=true
  idm.tenant=SM
  idm.token.signingKey=<your IdM signing key>
  idm.cookieName=IDM_AUTH_TOKEN

  idm.endpoint=https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service
  idm.http.user=idmTransportUser
  idm.http.password=<your password for the idmTransportUser user>

  idm.truststore=<customize-folder>/config/smrootca.p12 or /WEB-INF/smrootca.p12
  idm.truststore.password=<your password of smrootca.p12>
  idm.truststore.type=pkcs12

  idm.returnUri=https://apache.yourdomain.net/webtier

  isCustomAuthenticationUsed=false

For more information about how to set the appropriate values for common IdM parameters, see How to get IdM-related
settings.

            Note

                If there is no reverse proxy of load balancer exists on top of the web tier, you don't need to configure
                the idm.returnUri parameter.
                You MUST NOT enable LW-SSO at the same time. You need to revert the LW-SSO configuration if you have
                enabled LW-SSO before.
