1.8.17.4. Configure IdM authentication in Collaboration

You only need to update the chat server and chat service file to enable Identity Manager (IdM) authentication in Service
Manager Collaboration.

Enable IdM authentication in the chat server

To enable IdM authentication in the chat server, edit the <CHAT_SERVER>/conf/openfire.xml file. See the following
configuration as an example:

  <idmConfig>
      <ssoEnabled>true</ssoEnabled>
      <tokenSigningKey>your IdM signing key</tokenSigningKey>
      <cookieName>IDM_AUTH_TOKEN</cookieName>
      <tenant>SM</tenant>
      <endpoint>https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service</endpoint>
      <integrationUser>idmTransportUser</integrationUser>
      <integrationPassword>your password</integrationPassword>
      <trustAll>false</trustAll>
      <trustStorePath>../resources/security/smrootca.p12</trustStorePath>
      <trustStorePassword>caroot</trustStorePassword>
      <trustStoreType>pkcs12</trustStoreType>

  </idmConfig>

For more information, see IdM Parameters for Service Manager Collaboration.
For more information about how to set the appropriate values for common IdM parameters, see How to get IdM-related
settings.

Enable IdM authentication in the chat service

To enable IdM authentication in the chat service, edit the <CHAT_SERVICE>/conf/app.properties file. See the following
configuration as an example:

  idmConfig.ssoEnabled=true
  idmConfig.tokenSigningKey=<your IdM signing key>
  idmConfig.cookieName=IDM_AUTH_TOKEN
  idmConfig.tenant=SM
  idmConfig.endpoint=https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service
  idmConfig.integrationUser=idmTransportUser
  idmConfig.integrationPassword=<your password>
  idmConfig.trustAll=false
  idmConfig.trustStorePath=../conf/smrootca.p12
  idmConfig.trustStorePassword=caroot
  idmConfig.trustStoreType=pkcs12

For more information, see IdM Parameters for Service Manager Collaboration.

How to get IdM-related settings

Classic mode

The classic mode refers to a standalone Service Manager system that doesn't integrate with the SMA Service Portal.

Get the tenant

Use the name of the CONSUMER tenant you created when installing the IdM service.

Get the signing key

The signing key is the value you specified for the idm.encryptedSigningKey in the
system_resource_config__1.0.0.1__update_signingKey_and_initString.json seeded file when installing the IdM service. You
can also get the signing key from the IdM Admin Console. Go to SYSTEM SETTINGS, double-click the Encrypted signing key
property, and then check the value in the edit dialog.

Get the cookie name of the auth token

Use the default cookie name IDM_AUTH_TOKEN .

Get the service endpoint

Use the URL exposed by the reverse proxy or the load balancer (for example, https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service). If
there is no reverse proxy or load balancer on top of the IdM service, use the URL exposed by Tomcat (for example,

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026                                     Page 147 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

https://idmservice.yourdomain.net:8443/idm-service).
Get the password of idmTransportUser
The password is the value you entered in the Password field for the integration user when you created the SM tenant in the
IdM service.
Get the client truststore
Import your corporate root CA that issues the server certificate for the reverse proxy or the load balancer to a truststore by
using the certificate generation toolkit (for example, corprootca.p12 ). Use this truststore as the IdM client truststore.

  import-cert.bat --alias corprootca --file <your corporate root CA cert file> --keystore
  certs/corprootca.p12 --storepass <your password for corprootca.p12>

If you use the Service Manager private root CA to sign the server certificate for the reverse proxy in the dev environment, or
there is no reverse proxy or load balancer on top of the IdM service, use the smrootca.p12 as the IdM client truststore.

Mixed mode (SMA-SM)

The mixed mode refers to a Service Manager system that integrates with the SMA Service Portal.
Get the tenant
Use the ID of the Service Manager tenant you created when installing the SMA Service Portal and setting up the integration.
Get the signing key
If your SMA version is before 2023.05:
Get the signing key from Suite Administration. Go to CONFIGURATIONS > Security, and then check the value of the Signing
key field under IDM configuration.

If your SMA version is 2023.05 or higher, follow the steps below to get the IDM signing key:
   1. Log in to a control plane node or a worker node of SMA as the root or a sudo user.
   2. Run the following command to get the name of the bo-config pod:

          BO_CONFIG_POD=$(echo `kubectl get pods -n <SMA namespace> | grep -m1 itom-bo-config- | head
          -1 | awk '{print $1}'`) && echo $BO_CONFIG_POD

   3. Run the following command to get the IdM signing key:

          SIGNING_KEY=$(kubectl exec -it $BO_CONFIG_POD -n <SMA namespace> -c itom-bo-config -- bash
          -c "/bin/get_secret idm_token_signingkey_secret_key" | awk -F= '{print$2}') && echo
          $SIGNING_KEY

Get the cookie name of the auth token
Use the same cookie name defined by the SMA suite. For example, SMAX_AUTH_TOKEN .
Get the service endpoint
Use the URL exposed by the SMA suite. For example, https://smax.yourdomain.net/idm-service.
Get the password of idmTransportUser
Follow these steps to get the password of idmTransportUser :

   1. Sign in to one control plane node of SMA as root or a sudo user.
   2. Run the following command to identify the pod name for IdM.

          kubectl get pod -n <namespace> | grep ^idm

   3. Run the following command to go into the IdM pod.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 148 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

          kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -n <namespace> -c idm -- /bin/sh

   4. Run the following command to get the password of the transport user.

          get_secret idm_transport_user_password_secret_key

   5. Exit the pod.
Get the client truststore
Follow these steps to get the client truststore:

  1. Refer to the Get the suite CA certificate topic in the Service Management Automation - SM (SMA-SM) Help Center and
     get the SMA suite CA certificate ( <SMA cert file> ).

   2. Import the SMA suite CA certificate to a truststore by using the certificate generation toolkit (for example,
      suiterootca.p12 ), and then use this truststore as the IdM client truststore.

          import-cert.bat --alias suiterootca --file <SMA cert file> --keystore certs/suiterootca.p12
          --storepass <your password for suiterootca.p12>

1.8.18. SAML-based Single Sign-On

Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based, open-standard data format for exchanging authentication and
authorization data between parties. In particular, between an Identity Provider (IdP) and a Service Provider (SP). The single
most important requirement that SAML addresses is web browser single sign-on (SSO). SAML 2.0 is the industry standard for
federated identity management based on Single Sign-On (SSO).

            Tip

           SSO is a session or user authentication process that permits a user to enter the same name and password to
           access multiple web applications.

The SAML 2.0 specification defines an exhaustive list of profiles. By leveraging Identity Manager (IdM), Service Manager
support two essential profiles: Web Browser SSO Profile, and Single Logout Profile. The SAML SSO solution uses IdM as a
Service Provider and a third-party Identity Provider.

Benefits of using SAML SSO

By default, SAML SSO is disabled in Service Manager. When SAML SSO is enabled, if Service Manager shares the same IdP
and LDAP Server with other applications (whether the other applications leverage IdM or not), the user needs to enter a user
name and password only once to log in to all of these web applications. Additionally, this solution supports single logout for
multiple web applications that leverage IdM.

            Note

           Service Manager web tier, mobility client, and Collaboration support SAML SSO.

Using this solution has the following benefits:

     Provides tighter security controls through consistent enforcement of security policies across all applications
     Reduces turnaround time for provisioning and deprovisioning of user accounts in applications
     Fosters identity data collection, access reviews, and security analytics
     Provides single sign-on experience for end users
     Enables new users to gain faster access to the resources needed to perform their jobs
     Eliminates or reduces duplicate user IDs

Note that enabling SAML SSO may slow down user logins. According to laboratory tests by the company, user logins may
take approximately 15% more time.

Supported Identity Providers (IdPs)

Service Manager leverages the IdM service to support SAML-based SSO. The IdM service supports the following SAML 2.0-
compliant IdPs:

     Microsoft Active Directory Federation Services (ADFS) 3.0 or higher

This section uses Microsoft ADFS as an example for the IdP.

Prerequisites

     You must have a working ADFS and have synchronized the system clock with a reliable time source.
     You must have a working IdM service and have already integrated Service Manager with the IdM service. Refer to Install
     the IdM service and Configure IdM authentication in Service Manager for detailed instructions.

            Note

           Configurations in this section are for the classic mode. If you are working with the mixed mode (SMA-SM), refer
          to the Set up SAML authentication topic in the SMA-SM Help Center for detailed instructions.

Related topics

1.8.18.1. Overview of Service Manager SAML SSO

This section provides an overview of how the SAML SSO solution works for Service Manager (SM).

SP-initiated web browser SSO

The following diagram illustrates the web browser SSO process of Service Manager. In this process, the IdM service acts as
an SP to the IdP.

            Caution

           Use the standalone version of the IdM service released with Service Manager if you are not using SMA Service
           Portal. Otherwise, use the built-in IdM service in& SMA Service Portal.

The SM client (Web Tier or Mobility Client) uses a built-in IdM client as a filter to obtain an "IdM access token" from the IdM
service and then passes the token to the SM Server. The SM Server then validates the IdM access token.

            Note

           LDAP authentication is replaced by IdM; however, the LDAP data mapping is retained in the SM Server.

The following table further explains each step in this process.  Page 152 of 251

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026
                                                                             Service Manager 9.81

Step                                    Description

1                                       When the user launches the SM client (Web Tier or Mobility

                                        Client) web URL in the browser, the IdM Client embedded

                                        in the SM client sends a request to the IdM service for a

                                        request token.

2                                       The IdM service returns a response along with a request

                                        token to the built-in IdM client of the SM client (SM Web

                                        Tier or Mobility Client).

3                                       The IdM client redirects the request to the IdM service

                                        along with that token, and the IdM service then redirects it

                                        to the IdP login page with a SAML request.

4                                       The user enters a user name and password to log in to SM

                                        from the IdP login page.

                                                  Note

                                                  Users log in to Service Manager through the
                                                  IdP page, and their IdP login name is
                                                  determined by the IdP. That is, users need to
                                                  enter their login name using the format
                                                  required by the IdP. For example, when ADFS is
                                                  used as the IdP, the login name must be either
                                                  "userPrincipalName" (xxx@xxx.com) or
                                                  "domain\samAccountName".

5                                       The IdP redirects the request to the IdM service with a

                                        SAML response, and then the IdM service redirects the

                                        request to the SM client (Web Tier or Mobility Client) along

                                        with an "Access Token". Additionally, the IdM service

                                        writes a cookie named LWSSO_COOKIE_KEY to the

                                        browser.

6                                       The SM client (Web Tier or Mobility Client) logs in to the

                                        SM Server with that "Access Token".

7                                       The user is logged in to SM.

Web browser single logout

The SAML SSO solution supports single logout for legacy HPE web applications that leverage Identity Manager (IdM). Once
logged out of one application, the user is automatically logged out of the rest of the applications. This single logout behavior
applies to the SM Web Tier and Mobility Client.

Non-browser login

The SM Windows client and web service clients aren't browser-based applications. Login to SM from these clients is referred
to as "non-browser login", which doesn't support SAML. These clients log in to the SM Server through either a password or a
token. The token is an LW-SSO token when using the legacy LW-SSO solution or an IdM token when using the IdM solution.

     For password login, the login logic is the same as before. That is, the login process doesn't involve IdM.
     For LW-SSO token login, the SM Server provides a new interface for third- party applications to log in to SM using an
     IdM access token. The SM Server adds a new http header named “X-Idm-Token”, which contains the string value of the
     IdM access token.

Users must enter their login name that's determined by the LDAP field mapping on the SM side. For example, if the name field
in the SM operator table is mapped to the samAccountName field in ADFS, users must enter their samAccountName value

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026                                              Page 153 of 251
                                        Service Manager 9.81

as the login name.

1.8.18.2. Create a trusted relying party in ADFS

ADFS helps you use single sign-on (SSO) to authenticate users to multiple, related web applications over the life of a single
online session. Once ADFS is installed and configured to authenticate users from an LDAP directory, you are ready to add the
IdM metadata to ADFS to add the IdM service as a trusted relying party.

            Note

           The IdM service will automatically generate a self-signed certificate with one-year validity at the first startup for
           encrypting the SAML token. If you want to use a custom certificate for SAML authentication, you can configure
           the custom certificate before downloading the IdM SAML metadata. See Use a custom certificate for SAML
           authentication for detailed instructions.

Follow these steps to add the IdM service as a trusted relying party to ADFS:

   1. (Optional) Configure the SAML entity base URL.
     Skip this step if there is no reverse proxy or load balancer on top of the IdM service.
        1. Sign in to the IdM admin console (https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-admin) as a system administrator.
        2. Click GLOBAL SETTINGS, then click the SAML > Entity Base URL property, and then set the value to
           https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service.

   2. Download the IdM SAML metadata.
     Download the metadata from https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-service/saml/metadata. Save this file as
      idm_saml_metadata.xml , and then copy this file to the ADFS server.

   3. In the ADFS Management Console, click Add Relying Party Trust.

   4. Click Start.                      Page 155 of 251

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026
                                                                                         Service Manager 9.81

5. Select Import data about the relying party from a file, and then select the IdM metadata file ( idm_saml_metadata.xml )
  that you created previously. Click Next.

6. Specify a display name for the IdM service, and then add optional notes. Click Next.

1.8.18.3. Configure SAML authentication in IdM

To configure SAML authentication in IdM, follow these steps:
   1. Download the SAML metadata from the ADFS server (for example,
     https://adfs.yourdomain.net/FederationMetadata/2007-06/FederationMetadata.xml) and then save this file as
      FederationMetadata.xml .
   2. Sign in to the IdM admin console (https://apache.yourdomain.net/idm-admin) as a system administrator.
   3. Click the SM organization. Click Authentication > CONFIGURATIONS > Add (+), and then select the SAML
     authentication type to create an SAML authentication configuration. For example:
           Display Name: samlAuthConfig
           IDP Metadata: upload the FederationMetadata.xml file or copy its content to the text area on the right.

4. After you create the SAML authentication configuration, click Authentication > CONFIGURATION GROUPS > Add (+) to
  create a configuration group. For example:

        Name: saml
        Display Name: SAML Auth Group
        Configurations: samlAuthconfig

Verify the SAML SSO setup for Service Manager

Once you have completed all configurations required for SAML SSO, you are ready to verify if the setup is successful.
To verify the setup, follow these steps:

   1. Make sure all components are started, including the SM Server, client (web tier or Mobility Client), the standalone IdM
     service, and the identity provider (IdP, that is, ADFS).

   2. Launch the Service Manager web application URLs from a supported web browser (see the Service Manager Support
     Matrix).
           SM web tier URL: http://<web tier host>:<port>/<web tier name>/index.do
           Mobility Client URL: http://<Mobility Client host>:<port>/<Mobility application name>

   3. Verify that the browser redirects you to the IdP login page.
   4. Enter your username and password to sign in to one of the web applications.
   5. Verify that you are automatically signed in to the rest of the web applications without the need to enter your credentials.

                   Note

                ADFS doesn't allow you to select a login language. You are signed in to Service Manager with a language
                depending on which client you are using:

                      Web tier client: your browser language if the acceptBrowserLang parameter is set to true (default), or
                      your operator's language if this parameter is set to false
                      Mobility Client: your browser language
   6. Sign out of one of the Service Manager web applications.
   7. Verify that you are automatically signed out of the rest of the web applications.

            Tip

           If any of the verification steps fails, see Troubleshoot security.

1.8.18.4. Use a custom certificate for SAML authentication

Follow these steps to configure a custom certificate for SAML authentication.
   1. Create a self-signed certificate by using OpenSSL. For example, run the following command to create a self-signed
     certificate with 3 years validity.

          openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1095 -subj "/CN=IdM SAML Encryption" -

1.8.19. OIDC-based Single Sign-On

OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a simple identity layer on top of the OAuth protocol. It allows clients to verify the identity of the
end-user based on the authentication performed by an authorization server, as well as to obtain basic profile information
about the end-user in an interoperable and REST-like manner.
Users can access Service Manager after the OIDC configurations are completed. The user profile is synced to Service
Manager after the user signs in for the first time. If the user profile is updated in the identity provider, the updated information
will also be synced to Service Manager when the user signs in.

See Install Identity Manager (IdM) for detailed instructions.

1.8.20. Two-Factor Authentication

Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) is an extra layer of protection that you can use to ensure the security of Service Manager
accounts beyond just a username and password. It allows the Service Manager to verify the identity of the end-user based
on the authentication performed by an authorization server.
Service Manager leverages IdM authentication, and IdM authentication in turn leverages a third-party identity provider to
support 2FA authentication. The following diagram illustrates a simplified process of 2FA authentication.

The following diagram explicitly illustrates the 2FA authentication process of Service Manager with Azure AD as a sample IdP.
In this example, all components are deployed on the Cloud.

The following table further explains each step in this process.  Page 175 of 251

                                        client).

2                                       The SM client sends a request to the IdM service for a

                                        request token.

3                                       The IdM service returns a response along with a request

                                        token to the SM client.

4                                       The IdM client redirects the request to the IdM service

                                        along with that token, and then the IdM service redirects it

                                        to the Azure AD (IdP) login page with a SAML request.

5                                       The user enters a username and password to log in to SM

                                        from the Azure AD (IdP) login page. 1

                                        registered device (for example, a mobile phone).

1.8.21. FIPS mode

FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) are a set of standards that describe document processing, encryption
algorithms and other information technology standards for use within U.S. non-military government agencies and by U.S.
government contractors and vendors who work with the agencies.

FIPS 140-2, “Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules,” was issued by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and
Technology (NIST) in May, 2001. The standard specifies the security requirements for cryptographic modules utilized within a
security system that protects sensitive or valuable data.

For FIPS 140-2 compliance, Service Manager (SM) supports the implementation of FIPS validated AES-256 data encryption,
TLS connections and Lightweight Single Sign-On (LW-SSO), and FIPS compliant random number generation algorithms.

The following table describes two operation modes of the Service Manager server and clients.

Operation mode                          Description                             Notes

FIPS mode                               Supports FIPS 140-2 compliant
(FIPS 140-2 compliant mode)             cryptographic functions.

Non-FIPS mode                           Utilizes existing cryptography without
(Non-FIPS 140-2 compliant mode)         the 3rd-party FIPS 140-2 validated
                                        cryptographic modules.

In FIPS mode, Service Manager supports the same authentication methods as in non-FIPS mode. See the following table.

1.8.21.1. FIPS mode log messages

Service Manager writes FIPS mode related messages in the Server log and client log files.

Messages in the SM Server log

When FIPS mode is enabled on the Server side, the clients (Windows, Web Tier, Mobility, and Web Services) can connect to
the Server through https (either FIPS validated TLS or normal TLS); however, the recommended best security practice is to
run all of them in FIPS mode as well.
When FIPS mode is successfully enabled on the Server side, the following messages appear in the Server log
(Server\logs\sm.log):

  FIPS mode is set successfully.
  FIPS provider was initialized successfully.

Additionally, when FIPS mode is enabled on the Server side and the Windows Client is running in non-FIPS mode, the
following warning message appears in the Server log:

  Your Client is running in non-FIPS mode, but the Service Manager Server is running in FIPS
  mode. For the highest security, we recommend you enable FIPS mode for the Client.

            Note

           This message will also appear in the Windows Client user interface.

Messages in SM client logs

When FIPS mode is enabled successfully on the client sides, messages are written to the client logs. See the following table.

1.8.21.2. Limitations of FIPS mode

The following limitation exist in the support of FIPS mode for Service Manager (SM).

Service Manager initialization might be slow in Linux environments

This issue may occur when fipsmode:2 is specified in the SM Server's sm.ini file. It is caused by a lack of entropy
(randomness) available on the system used for random number generation and can commonly occur on systems that aren't
receiving much direct user input, such as virtual machines.
As a workaround, you can direct the JVM to use /dev/urandom with the following directive:

     Add the following line to the Server's sm.ini file:

          JVMOption0:-Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom

     Alternatively, you can add the following line to the jre/lib/security/java.security file:

          securerandom.source=file:/dev/./urandom

For additional information, see the following important third-party information:
http://bugs.java.com/view_bug.do?bug_id=6521844
http://www.2uo.de/myths-about-urandom/

FIPS mode

1.8.21.4. Configuring FIPS mode in Service Manager

For the best security, you can configure FIPS mode in Service Manager (SM) to implement FIPS 140-2 validated
TLS connections in the entire system.

            Note

           Once FIPS mode is enabled on the SM Server side (that is, fipsmode:2 is specified in the sm.ini file), clients
           running in non-FIPS mode are still allowed to connect to the SM Server through normal SSL. However, for the best
           security, this is not recommended.

To enable FIPS mode in Service Manager, perform the following steps in the listed order:

   1. Configure Java and web application servers for FIPS mode
   2. Generate FIPS validated certificates for the SM Server and other components
   3. Configure FIPS mode in the Server
   4. Configure FIPS mode in the Windows Client
   5. Configure FIPS mode in the Web Tier
   6. Configure FIPS mode in the Mobility Client
   7. Configure FIPS mode in the Chat Server
   8. Configure FIPS mode in the Chat Service
   9. Configure FIPS mode in the IdM Service

Additionally, if you need to use LW-SSO, you can configure Service Manager to use FIPS validated LW-SSO. For detailed
instructions, see Configuring LW-SSO in FIPS mode.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 186 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

1.8.21.4.1. Configure Java and web application servers for
FIPS mode

The Service Manager web tier, mobility, and IdM service are deployed on web application servers. You need to first configure
Java security providers and web application servers for FIPS mode, and then configure FIPS mode for individual SM
components.

            Note

           You don't need to manually configure Java security providers for the SM server, chat server, chat service, and
           Windows client. These components will automatically configure Java security providers when you enable FIPS
           mode for them.

Prerequisites

Before you proceed, make sure of the following:

   1. You have installed Java 17 and web application servers.
   2. You have already generated a server certificate file for web application servers. For details, see Generate FIPS validated

     certificates for the SM Server and other components.

Configure Java security provider

You need to configure the java security properties file to use the BCFIPS security provider as the default security provider.

   1. Create a folder to store FIPS-related files (for example, C:\FIPS ). This topic refers to this folder as <FIPS_HOME> in
     later steps.

   2. Copy the bc-fips-<version>.jar file from the <TOMCAT_HOME>/webapps/<appname>/WEB-INF/lib folder to the
      <FIPS_HOME> folder. Note that the <appname> may be webtier , mobility , or idmservice .

   3. Copy the java.security file from the <JAVA_HOME>/conf/security folder to the <FIPS_HOME> folder.
   4. Edit the <FIPS_HOME>/java.security file.

        1. Add BCFIPS provider as the first security provider, and update provider ID for subsequent providers.
        2. Enable FIPS mode for SunJSSE by specifying a BCFIPS crypto provider for it.
        3. Set the default keystore type to bcfks .
     For example:

          ...
          security.provider.1=BCFIPS C:DEFRND[CTRAES256];ENABLE{ALL};
          security.provider.2=SUN
          security.provider.3=SunRsaSign
          security.provider.4=SunEC
          security.provider.5=SunJSSE BCFIPS
          security.provider.6=SunJCE
          security.provider.7=SunJGSS
          security.provider.8=SunSASL
          security.provider.9=XMLDSig
          security.provider.10=SunPCSC
          security.provider.11=JdkLDAP
          security.provider.12=JdkSASL
          security.provider.13=SunMSCAPI
          security.provider.14=SunPKCS11
          ...
          keystore.type=bcfks
          ...

Configure Tomcat

You need to configure Tomcat to use the customized java.security file by setting appropriate JVM options.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 187 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

If you start Tomcat by running the script file ( startup.bat or startup.sh ), you need to first create the setenv.bat or
setenv.sh file in the <TOMCAT_HOME>/bin folder, and then add JVM options to the setenv.bat or setenv.sh file. For
example:
Windows ( setenv.bat ):

  set FIPS_HOME=<FIPS_HOME>
  set FIPS_OPTS=--module-path=%FIPS_HOME% --add-
  opens=java.base/sun.security.internal.spec=org.bouncycastle.fips.core
  set FIPS_OPTS=%FIPS_OPTS% -Djava.security.properties==%FIPS_HOME%\java.security -
  Dorg.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only=true
  set JAVA_OPTS=%JAVA_OPTS% %FIPS_OPTS%

Linux ( setenv.sh ):

  #!/bin/sh
  FIPS_HOME=<FIPS_HOME>
  FIPS_OPTS="--module-path=${FIPS_HOME} --add-
  opens=java.base/sun.security.internal.spec=org.bouncycastle.fips.core"
  FIPS_OPTS="${FIPS_OPTS} -Djava.security.properties==${FIPS_HOME}/java.security -
  Dorg.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only=true"
  JAVA_OPTS="${JAVA_OPTS} ${FIPS_OPTS}"

If you install Tomcat as a Windows service, start the tomcat9w.exe, switch to the Java tab, and then add the following JVM
options to the Java Options list. For example:

  --module-path=<FIPS_HOME>
  --add-opens=java.base/sun.security.internal.spec=org.bouncycastle.fips.core
  -Djava.security.properties==<FIPS_HOME>\java.security
  -Dorg.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only=true

Next, copy the cacerts file and the Tomcat server certificate keystore file from cert-utils to the <TOMCAT_HOME>/conf
folder. Edit the <TOMCAT_HOME>/conf/server.xml file to configure the truststore and the keystore for the https connector.
For example:

  ...
  <Connector port="8443" protocol="org.apache.coyote.http11.Http11NioProtocol"

                      maxThreads="150" SSLEnabled="true">

         <SSLHostConfig truststoreFile="conf/cacerts"
                                     truststorePassword="changeit"
                                     truststoreType="bcfks">

                 <Certificate certificateKeystoreFile="conf/tomcat.bcfks"
                                        certificateKeystorePassword="serverkeystore"
                                        certificateKeystoreType="bcfks" />

         </SSLHostConfig>
  </Connector>
  ...

1.8.21.4.2. Generate FIPS validated certificates for the
SM Server and other components

Before you can enable FIPS mode in the Service Manager (SM) system, you must obtain a CA certificates file and keystore
files in BCFKS format (with the .bcfks file extension) for the SM Server and other components. These certificates are used for
FIPS validated TLS connections between the SM Server and other components.

            Note

           In a production environment, you are recommended to use digital security certificates issued by a certificate
           authority provider, such as Verisign, Thawte, or your corporate certificate authority. The digital certificate
           contains a public key, the identity of the owner, and a matching private key. The certificate is required to encrypt
           data sent and received in a “trusted” environment. If you don't have a digital certificate from a provider listed
           above, you have the option of generating your own certificates to enable encrypted data transfer between the
           Service manager Server and the trusted clients, as described in the following.

     Existing customers need to either convert your existing certificates to BCFKS format or regenerate new BCFKS
     certificates.

                   Caution

                The SM Server truststore and trusted clients keystore don't contain a private key, and can work correctly in
                FIPS mode after conversion to BCFKS format. However, the SM server keystore and client keystores contain
                a private key. Before converting them to BCFKS format, make sure their private key was created using either
                "keytool -genkey -keyalg RSA" or "keytool -genkeypair -keyalg RSA"; otherwise they can't work correctly in
                FIPS mode after conversion to BCFKS format. Before you proceed, make sure the private key of the existing
                JKS file was created as noted above. If not, you will need to generate a new BCFKS certificate.

     New customers need to generate BCFKS certificates for the SM Server and clients (Windows, Web Tier, and Mobility).

As a courtesy, we provide a certificate generation toolkit to help you generate certificates for a Service Manager deployment
in an automated way. For details, see Work with the certificate generation toolkit.

Configure FIPS mode in the Server

1.8.21.4.3. Configure FIPS mode in the Server

By default, FIPS mode is disabled, and Service Manager uses the 64-bit DES data encryption algorithm and supports non-
FIPS validated SSL/TLS connections. To run Service Manager in FIPS mode, you need to enable FIPS validated data
encryption and TLS connections.

Prerequisites

Before you proceed, make sure you have already generated the following certificate files for the SM Server. For details, see
Work with the certificate generation toolkit.

     The CA certificates file: \certs\cacerts
     The Server's trusted clients keystore file: \certs\trustedclients.bcfks
     The Server keystore file: \certs\smserver.bcfks
To enable FIPS mode in the SM Server, complete the following tasks.

            Caution

           To enable FIPS mode in a scaling environment, you must configure FIPS mode in each of the SM server nodes.

Steps to enable FIPS mode for data encryption

After enabling FIPS mode, you must upgrade your database's encryption algorithm from DES to AES by running the sm -
upgradeencralg command.

   1. Make a backup of your database.

                   Caution

                FIPS mode requires the database to upgrade to the 256-bit AES encryption algorithm. Because the upgrade
                is irreversible, you need to make a backup of your database.

   2. Check the length of each encrypted field in your database, and increase the length if needed.

                   Tip

                Use the following formula to determine a safe length for an AES encrypted field (in bytes):

                        Safe_Length=32 + 2 * source_string_length

                Where: source_string_length is the length of the source string (for example, if you enter an 8-character
                password, the source string length is 8 bytes).

   3. Upgrade your applications to the AES data encryption algorithm.
     FIPS mode requires the use of the 256-bit AES data encryption algorithm for the database. By default, the Service
     Manager applications uses the 64-bit Data Encryption Standard (DES) encryption algorithm. You must upgrade the
     database from the DES encryption algorithm to AES by running the sm -upgradeencralg command.

                   Caution

                This algorithm upgrade is required only when you want to enable FIPS mode.

          a. Make sure you can connect to the server successfully.
          b. Make sure all Service Manager server processes are stopped.
          c. Check that the server's configuration file ( sm.ini ) doesn't include the fipsmode parameter.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 192 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

          d. From <Servcie Manager installation directory>/Server/Run, run the sm -upgradeencralg command.

                        Note

                     If you have many tables with encrypted fields, running this command may take quite a while; if you have
                     already run this command on the database, running it again will have no effect and do no harm to the
                     database.

                        Tip

                     You can specify a 32-character alphanumeric value for this parameter, as the new encryption key; if you
                     don't specify any value, a default 32-character (256-bit) encryption key is used. You can also change
                     your encryption key later using the changeencrkey parameter.

          e. Check the server log (sm.log) for any errors.

Steps to enable FIPS mode for TLS connections

Follow these steps:
   1. Copy the certificate files listed in the previous step to the SM Server's RUN directory:
          • The CA certificates file: \certs\cacerts
          • The Server's trusted clients keystore file: trustedclients.bcfks
          • The Server keystore file: smserver.bcfks
   2. Add the following parameters to the sm.ini file in the Server's RUN folder.

                   Caution

                The example certificate file names and passwords used in the following lines are the default ones specified
                in the certificate generation batch files provided by the company. For details, see Generate FIPS validated
                certificates for the SM Server and other components. If you use different file names or passwords when
                generating your certificates, be sure to replace them with your own values.

                   Tip

                The ciphers and sslEnabledProtocols parameters are specified here with their default values. Since
                Service Manager will use their default values when the two parameters aren't present in the sm.ini file, you
                can omit them safely. These parameters are provided just in case you don't want to use their default values.

          fipsmode:2
          ssl:1
          sslConnector:1
          ssl_reqClientAuth:2
          keystoreFile:smserver.bcfks
          keystorePass:serverkeystore
          ssl_trustedClientsJKS:trustedclients.bcfks
          ssl_trustedClientsPwd:trustedclients
          truststoreFile:cacerts
          truststorePass:changeit
          ciphers:TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384,TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256,TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA3
          84,TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256,TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384,TLS_ECDHE_
          RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
          sslEnabledProtocols:TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3
          JVMOption1:-Djdk.tls.ephemeralDHKeySize=2048

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 193 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

                   Note

                When running under JDK 8, the JDK's SunJSSE TLS implementation is unable to negotiate a TLS handshake
                when using an ECDHE cipher suite.

   3. Go to the <Service Manager server installation path>/RUN folder, and open lwssofmconf.xml in a text editor.
   4. Locate the following section:

          <lwssoValidation>
          <domain>yourdomain.net</domain>
          <crypto cipherType="symmetricBlockCipher"
          engineName="AES" paddingModeName="CBC" keySize="256"
          encodingMode="Base64Url"
          initString="This is a shared secret passphrase"/>
          <!-- When Service Manager is running in FIPS mode, the crypto configuration above needs to
          be replaced with the configuration below. The initString value must be 32 characters long
          and contain no spaces. -->
          <!--
          <crypto cryptoSource="jce" cipherType="symmetricBlockCipher"
          engineName="AES" paddingModeName="CBC" keySize="256"
          pbeDigestAlgorithm="SHA1" encodingMode="Base64Url"
          jcePbeAlgorithmName="AES" jcePbeMacAlgorithmName="AES"
          macType="hmac"
          macAlgorithmName="SHA1" directKeyEncoded="true" directKeyEncoding="Base64Url"
          algorithmPaddingName="PKCS5Padding"
          pbeCount="20" macKeySize="256" macPbeCount="20"
          initString="rqa9mkdmfkvdvienfj4usldo9205mvid">
          </crypto>
          -->
          </lwssoValidation>

     Comment out the ordinary crypto configuration part, and then uncomment the FIPS mode crypto configuration part.
     Note: Please make sure that the value of initString is complied with the encoding rule defined for directKeyEncoding
     in the section above.
     When Service Manager starts, the system loads the LW-SSO related jar files and verifies the algorithms that are related
     to LW-SSO configuration. Based on the verification result, the system judges whether Service Manager is running in
     FIPS mode or not. Hence, to ensure Service Manager is running in FIPS mode, you must switch the crypto configuration
     in lwssofmconf.xml to the one as FIPS mode required.
     Note: Do not change the domain setting in this file unless you are configuring LW-SSO.

          <domain>yourdomain.net</domain>

   5. Restart the SM Server.
     Next, you need to enable FIPS mode in the Windows Client to verify that your FIPS mode is successfully enabled on the
     Server side.

1.8.21.4.4. Configure FIPS mode in the Windows Client

Once you have enabled FIPS mode on the Service Manager (SM) Server side, you need to enable FIPS mode in the Windows
Client and test if the Windows Client can connect to the SM Server successfully.

Prerequisites

Before you proceed, make sure of the following:

   1. You have already generated a CA certificates file and a client keystore for the Windows Client host. For details, see
     Generate FIPS validated certificates for the SM Server and other components.
           The CA certificates file: \certs\smrootca.bcfks
           The Windows Client keystore file: \certs\<Windows Client alias defined in certs.conf>.bcfks (for example,
           james.jones.bcfks)

   2. You have enabled FIPS mode on the SM Server side. For details, see Configure FIPS mode in the Server.

Steps to enable FIPS mode in the Windows Client

To configure FIPS mode in the Windows Client, follow these steps:

   1. Copy the CA certificates file and client keystore file to a directory on the Windows Client host:
           smrootca.bcfks
           james.jones.bcfks

   2. Configure the Windows Client preferences.
        1. Start the Windows client, and click Window > Preferences > Service Manager > Security.
        2. Select the FIPS Mode checkbox.
           A message appears, indicating that you need to restart the Windows Client to continue.
           Click OK to exit the message window.
           Because the Windows Client is hardcoded to use the RSA BSAFE JsafeJCE provider for FIPS mode, you no longer
           need to specify a cryptographic provider. For this reason, the following parameters are disabled (grayed out) when
           the FIPS Mode option is selected:
                 JCE provider name
                 JCE provider class name

                         Tip

                      These parameters are used to specify a third-party Java Cryptography Extension (JCE) provider when
                      the Windows Client is running in non-FIPS mode (that is, when the FIPS Mode checkbox is not
                      selected).

           Note that the following parameters are also disabled at this point, because a restart of the Windows Client is
           needed after the FIPS Mode option is enabled. After a restart, these parameters will be available to configure in the
           Preferences window.

                 CA certificates password
                 Client keystore password
           The following screenshot illustrates the Preferences window when FIPS Mode is selected.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 195 of 251
                                                                                                                                                           Service Manager 9.81

        Click OK again to exit the Preferences window.
        Close the Windows Client.
3. Restart the Windows Client.
4. Click Window > Preferences > Service Manager > Security.
5. Configure the parameters as described in the following.
  Click Browse to enter the CA certificates file, and then enter the password in the CA certificates password field.
  Click Browse to enter the client keystore file, and then enter the password in the Client keystore password field.
  Click Apply, and then click OK twice.

6. Click File to open your client connection, and do the following to verify the SM Server and Windows Client have
  FIPS mode enabled correctly:

     1. Select the Use Login/Password option on the Connection tab.

     2. Check that the Use SSL Encryption option on the Advanced tab is selected and grayed out.

                         Note

                      When the FIPS Mode option is enabled, the Windows Client is forced to use SSL encryption.

        3. Enter your user name and password.
        4. In the Server host name field, enter the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of the SM Server.
        5. In the Server port number field, enter the HTTP port (for example, 13080) of the SM Server.
        6. Click Connect.
     If FIPS mode has been successfully enabled in the SM Server and Windows Client, you should be successfully logged
     in.

1.8.21.4.5. Configure FIPS mode in the Web Tier

Once you have enabled FIPS mode on the Service Manager (SM) Server side, you need to enable FIPS mode in the Web Tier.

Prerequisites

     You have configured Java security providers and web application servers for FIPS mode. For details, see Configure

     is not set in the web.xml, and then append the following scripts to the <WEBTIER>/WEB-INF/webtier.properties file.

          fipsMode=true
          ssl=true
          keystore=/WEB-INF/smwebtier.bcfks
          keystorePassword=clientkeystore
          cacerts=/WEB-INF/smrootca.bcfks
          cacertsPassword=caroot
          cookie.secure=true

   2. Go to the <web tier root>/WEB-INF/classes folder, and open lwssofmconf.xml in a text editor.
   3. Locate the following section:

1.8.21.4.9. Configure FIPS mode in the IdM Service

To enable the FIPS mode in the IdM service, you need to make some additional configurations when you install the IdM
service. Content in this topic is supplementary to Install Identity Manager (IdM).

Prerequisites

Before you proceed, make sure that you have configured Java security providers and Tomcat for FIPS mode. For details, see
Configure Java and web application servers for FIPS mode.

Task 1: Configure the IdM Service

You need to configure the IdM service to use the BCFIPS security provider and configure the default truststore.
   1. Edit the WEB-INF/classes/idm-security.properties file to enable FIPS mode and set the truststore. For example:

          useExternalProvider=true
          sslTruststore=<TOMCAT_HOME>/conf/cacerts
          sslTruststorePassword=changeit

   2. Edit the WEB-INF/classes/security/key-configuration.properties file to use the BCFIPS security provider. For example:

          enckeytype.local.profile=strong256bit
          enckeytype.local.jce=BCFIPS
          enckeytype.local.keyfile=key-local-strong256.bin
          enckeytype.local.passphrase.name=local strong256 passphrase
          enckeytype.local.passphrase.provider=file
          enckeytype.local.passphrase.file=key-local-strong256-passphrase.txt
          enckeytype.local.passphrase.deleteFile=false

          enckeytype.network.profile=strong256bit
          enckeytype.network.jce=BCFIPS
          enckeytype.network.keyfile=key-network-strong256.bin
          enckeytype.network.passphrase.name=network strong256 passphrase
          enckeytype.network.passphrase.provider=file
          enckeytype.network.passphrase.file=key-network-strong256-passphrase.txt
          enckeytype.network.passphrase.deleteFile=false

   3. Add more LW-SSO settings to the system_resource_config__1.0.0.1__update_signingKey_and_initString.json seeded
     json file.
     For example:

1.8.21.5. Configuring LW-SSO in FIPS mode

When running in FIPS mode, the Service Manager (SM) Server, Web Tier, Mobility Client, and Openfire Chat Server use a FIPS
validated cryptographic provider for Lightweight Single Sign-On (LW-SSO).
When Service Manager is running in FIPS mode, the following rules apply for web services clients (integrations):

     It is recommended to enable FIPS mode for the web service clients as well.
     Web service clients that don't support FIPS mode can still integrate with SM through normal TLS connections.
     LW-SSO will not work if the web service client doesn't support FIPS mode.

For more information about the support of FIPS mode for the products that can integrate with SM, see the documentation of
the specific products. This document covers only SM components.
The steps to configure LW-SSO in SM for FIPS mode are the same as for non-FIPS mode, except the cryptographic provider
configuration part. The steps are described in the following tasks:
Configure LW-SSO in the Server for FIPS mode
Configure LW-SSO in the Web tier for FIPS mode
Configure LW-SSO in the Mobility Client for FIPS mode
Configure LW-SSO in the Chat Server for FIPS mode
Configure LW-SSO in the Chat Service for FIPS mode

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 209 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

1.8.21.5.1. Configure LW-SSO in the Server for FIPS mode

Applies to User roles: System Administrator
Enabling LW-SSO in the Service Manager (SM) Server enables web service integrations from legacy HPE products to bypass
Service Manager authentication if the product user is already authenticated and a proper token is used; enabling LW-SSO in
both the Service Manager Server and Web Tier enables users to bypass the login prompts when launching the Service
Manager web client from legacy HPE applications.

            Caution

           To use LW-SSO, your Service Manager Web Tier and Server must be deployed in the same domain; therefore you
           should use the same domain name for the Web Tier and Server. If you fail to do so, users who log in from another
           application to the web tier can log in but may be forcibly logged out after a while.

Prerequisite:
Before you proceed, make sure you have enabled FIPS mode on the Service Manager Server side. For detailed instructions,
see Configure FIPS mode in the Server.
To configure LW-SSO in the Service Manager server for FIPS mode, follow these steps:

   1. Go to the <Service Manager server installation path>/RUN folder, and open lwssofmconf.xml in a text editor.
   2. Make sure that the enableLWSSOFramework attribute is set to true (default).
   3. Locate the following section.

          <lwssoValidation>
          <domain>yourdomain.net</domain>
          <crypto cipherType="symmetricBlockCipher"
          engineName="AES" paddingModeName="CBC" keySize="256"
          encodingMode="Base64Url"
          initString="This is a shared secret passphrase"/>
          <!-- When Service Manager is running in FIPS mode, the crypto configuration above needs to
          be replaced with the configuration below. The initString value must be 32 characters long
          and contain no spaces. -->
          <!--
          <crypto cryptoSource="jce" cipherType="symmetricBlockCipher"
          engineName="AES" paddingModeName="CBC" keySize="256"
          pbeDigestAlgorithm="SHA1" encodingMode="Base64Url"
          jcePbeAlgorithmName="AES" jcePbeMacAlgorithmName="AES"
          macType="hmac"
          macAlgorithmName="SHA1" directKeyEncoded="true" directKeyEncoding="Base64Url"
          algorithmPaddingName="PKCS5Padding"
          pbeCount="20" macKeySize="256" macPbeCount="20"
          initString="rqa9mkdmfkvdvienfj4usldo9205mvid">
          </crypto>
          -->
          </lwssoValidation>

   4. Update this section by doing the following:
           Comment out the ordinary crypoto configuration part.
           Uncomment the FIPS mode crypto configuration part.
           Configure the domain of the host.
           Update the default initString value to your own value, if needed.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 210 of 251
                                                                                                                                                       Service Manager 9.81

                   Caution

                The initString value is shared among all parties that participate in LW-SSO. In FIPs mode, this value
                must be 32 characters long and contain no spaces; otherwise LW-SSO will not work in FIPS mode.

The following is an example:

  <lwssoValidation>
  <domain>myhostdomain.com</domain>
  <!--
  <crypto cipherType="symmetricBlockCipher"
  engineName="AES" paddingModeName="CBC" keySize="256"
  encodingMode="Base64Url"
  initString="This is a shared secret passphrase"/>
  -->
  <!-- When Service Manager is running in FIPS mode, the crypto configuration above needs to
  be replaced with the configuration below.
  The initString value must be 32 characters long and contain no spaces. -->
  <crypto cryptoSource="jce" cipherType="symmetricBlockCipher"
  engineName="AES" paddingModeName="CBC" keySize="256"
  pbeDigestAlgorithm="SHA1" encodingMode="Base64Url"
  jcePbeAlgorithmName="AES" jcePbeMacAlgorithmName="AES"
  macType="hmac"
  macAlgorithmName="SHA1" directKeyEncoded="true" directKeyEncoding="Base64Url"
  algorithmPaddingName="PKCS5Padding"
  pbeCount="20" macKeySize="256" macPbeCount="20"
  initString="1qaz2wsxfkvdvienfj4usldo9205mvid">
  </crypto>
  </lwssoValidation>

            Note

           Here, myhostdomain.com refers to the domain of the SM Server host.

      Note

           You're not recommended to modify the paddingModeName , keySize , encodingMode , engineName ,
           and cipherType attributes. If you need to modify them, be careful to ensure security and make sure that
           they are same with the LW-SSO settings of the other legacy HPE product that you want to integrate with
           Service Manager.
           Do not change the other configurations, such as the content in tag <restURLs> , and the attribute of tag
           <service> .

1.8.21.5.2. Configure LW-SSO on the web tier for FIPS mode

Applies to User roles: System Administrator
If Lightweight Single Sign-On (LW-SSO) is enabled on the Service Manager web tier, integrations from legacy HPE products
will bypass Service Manager authentication when launching the Service Manager Web client, provided that the user of the
legacy HPE product is already authenticated and a proper token is used.

            Note

                To enable users to launch the Web client from another legacy HPE product using LW-SSO, you must also
                enable LW-SSO in the Service Manager server.
                Once you have enabled LW-SSO in the web tier, web client users should use the web tier server's fully-
                qualified domain name (FQDN) in the login URL: http://<myWebtierHostName>.<myDomain>:
                <port>/webtier-x.xx/index.do
                The following procedure is provided as an example, assuming that the Service Manager web tier is deployed
                on Tomcat.

Prerequisite

     Before you proceed, make sure you have enabled FIPS mode on the web tier. For detailed instructions, see Configure
     FIPS mode on the web tier.

                         Note

                      This is required to enable LW-SSO from the web tier to the server.

        3. Change the value of context parameter isCustomAuthenticationUsed to false.

                 <param-value>false</param-value>
                 </context-param>

1.8.22. Tokenization

The Service Manager web tier has tokenization enabled by default. Enabling tokenization helps safeguard sensitive data.
When tokenization is enabled, the web tier appends a token to URLs and checks requested URLs that contain any predefined
actions or match any predefined patterns to see if they have the token appended; if the token is not found, the web tier
returns an error.
Administrators can also disable this feature by turning off a parameter in the web tier configuration file ( web.xml ).

Related parameters

Three web.xml parameters are used for tokenization (see the following table). Out-of-the-box, the simpleURLs and
patterns parameters aren't present in the web.xml file. If you don't add them, their default values take effect.

            Note

           To enable tokenization, enabling the antiCSRFEnabled parameter is enough. Adding the other parameters is
           unnecessary unless you need to change their values from the default ones.

1.9.1. Defining batch sizes in the counters file

Administrators can allocate blocks of record identifiers for each servlet in horizontal and vertical scaling implementations. By
allocating record IDs in advance, administrators can reduce traffic between the Service Manager server and the RDBMS,
which improves overall system performance.

Note: Setting a batch size value replaces the fastcounters parameter from previous versions.

Administrators allocate record IDs in batches from the counters file. When you define a batch size, Service Manager
retrieves that number of ID keys from the RDBMS and stores the keys in shared memory for later use. Each time someone
creates a new record, the system assigns it an ID key from shared memory until there are no more IDs available. Once the
system exhausts its supply of IDs, it requests the next batch of IDs from the RDBMS. Allocating IDs in advance improves
performance, because retrieving the reserved ID keys from shared memory is more efficient than connecting to the RDBMS
and requesting a new ID key with every new record.

Batch file size recommendation

We recommend you set the batch file size to the number of new records you expect users to create in an hour divided by the
number of servers in the implementation. For example, if you expect to generate 200 incident records an hour and have only
one server in your implementation, then set the Batch Size value to 200. If your system consists of multiple servers, such as
in a horizontal scaling implementation, then divide the total records per hour by the number of servers. For example, a
horizontal scaling implementation with four servers only needs a batch size of 50 for each server to equal 200 incidents per
hour.

Note: In a horizontally scaled system, each server requests its own batch of ID keys. Since new records may be created from
processes running on different servers in a horizontal scaling implementation, the ID numbers of new records may not be in
sequential order. For example, process A on server 1 has reserved ID keys 1-100 and process B on server 2 has reserved ID
keys 101-200. The first record a user creates on process A will have ID 1, but if the very next record created comes from
process B, then the ID will be 101, not 2.

If you don't specify a batch size value, Service Manager uses the default batch size of 1 and fetches a new ID from the
RDBMS for each new record you create.

Example data from a counters file

TABLE_NAME COLUMN_NAME CURRENT_VALUE BATCH_SIZE

schedule schedule.id 2587564            1000

Related topics

1.9.2. Defining record identifiers in batches using the
numbers file

Administrators can define record identifiers and allocate those identifiers in batches from the numbers file for new
interactions, incidents, and changes. By allocating record IDs in batches in advance, administrators can reduce traffic
between the Service Manager server and the RDBMS, which improves overall system performance.

            Note

Currently the counters file is used by administrators to define the table and field where a new record number is
going to be stored. However, the numbers file is still available for those who previously chose to define record
numbers using the numbers file and are upgrading. This file has been enhanced to work more like the counters
file. For more information on the counters file, see the related topics.

When using the numbers file, administrators define the following:

     Batch size.
     Starting number.
     Identifying prefix for each module. For example, IM for Incident Management records.
     Whether numbers are going to increment or decrement.
     The table and field where the new numbers are to be stored.

When you define a batch size, Service Manager retrieves that number of ID keys from the RDBMS and stores the keys in
shared memory for later use. Each time someone creates a new record, the system assigns it an ID key from shared memory
until there are no more IDs available. Once the system exhausts its supply of IDs, it requests the next batch of IDs from the
RDBMS.

We recommend you set the batch file size to the number of new records you expect users to create in an hour, divided by the
number of servers in the implementation. For example, if you expect to generate 200 incident records an hour and have only
one server in your implementation, then set the Batch Size value to 200. If your system consists of multiple servers, such as
in a horizontal scaling implementation, then divide the total records per hour by the number of servers. For example, a
horizontal scaling implementation with four servers only needs a batch size of 50 for each server to equal 200 incidents per
hour.

In a horizontally scaled system, each server requests its own batch of ID keys. Since new records may be created from
processes running on different servers in a horizontal scaling implementation, the ID numbers of new records may not be in
sequential order. For example, process A on server 1 has reserved ID keys 1-100 and process B on server 2 has reserved ID
keys 101-200. The first record a user creates on process A will have ID 1, but if the very next record created comes from
process B, then the ID will be 101, not 2.

If you don't specify a batch size value, Service Manager uses the default batch size of 1 and fetches a new ID from the
RDBMS for each new record you create.

1.9.3. Lock Management

The locking mechanism in versions of Service Manager (SM) prior to version 9.31 had a locking mechanism that used a
multicasting to request and obtain a lock on a resource in Service Manager. This locking mechanism was implemented using
a Peer Lock in the JGroups toolkit. However, there were several issues with this implementation, which are addressed with
the new locking mechanism introduced in this document.

Issues in Service Manager Multicast Communication

Service Manager’s previous multicast implementation suffers from the following limitations:

• All nodes must be contacted by the node that's requesting the resource. This leads to high overhead per request.

• All nodes must give approval to a request, regardless of whether a node is using a resource or not.

• A node that doesn't respond represents a single point of failure for the system, even if that node has no other connection to
the resource or the requesting node.
• If one node doesn't respond, the request must be re-issued by the originating node, which increases overhead even
further.

• Nodes that are slow to respond will eventually be removed from the node cluster.

• Scalability is very poor.

• The potential for netstorms is high (wherein every node is attempting to request permission from every other node, leading
to n^2 requests).

New Locking Mechanism Overview

The new locking mechanism consists of a record entry for each locked resource in a database table. The new Lock table (for
exclusive locks) and LockShared table (for shared locks) have been created to house these records. See the following tables
for details on the structure and fields of the Lock and LockShared tables.

Note: The only difference between these two tables is the value in the TYPE field, and the primary key for the LockShared
table is a combination of the LOCKID, pID, tID, and IP fields.

Lock Behavior

Locks may be either shared locks or exclusive locks. A shared lock allows multiple nodes to read the data from a resource.
An exclusive lock may only be obtained if any shared locks on a resource have been released by the nodes that hold them.

Exclusive Lock

The process by which a node obtains an exclusive lock is as follows:

   1. A node that requests an exclusive lock tries to insert a record into the Lock database table to see whether a resource is
     available.

   2. If there is no record for this resource in the Lock table, the resource is available and the node holder obtains the lock
     and inserts a record into the Lock table.

   3. If there is a record in the Lock table, the node will fail to obtain a lock.

To unlock an exclusive lock, the corresponding lock record is removed from the Lock table.

Shared Lock

The process by which a node obtains a shared lock is as follows:

   1. A node that requests a shared lock tries to insert a record into the Lock database table to see whether a resource is
     available.

   2. If there is no record for this resource in the Lock table, the node holder inserts a record into the Lock table and proceeds
     to step 4.

   3. If there is a record in the Lock table, the TYPE field of that record is checked. If the TYPE field is “Exclusive” the lock
     requested is rejected. If the TYPE field is “Shared,” proceed to step 4.

   4. The node tries to insert a record into the LockShared table. If the insertion is successful, the shared lock request is
     granted. If the insertion fails, the shared lock request is rejected.

To unlock a shared lock, the corresponding lock record is removed from the LockShared table. Then, the corresponding lock
record is removed from the Lock table unless other records share the same resource ID.

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026                      Page 232 of 251
                                                                                                                                                               Service Manager 9.81

Note: There is no mechanism to escalate a Shared lock to an Exclusive lock. To obtain an exclusive lock on a resource, all
shared locks must be released.

Lock Retry, Timeout, and Heartbeat

Each process that requires a lock has a dedicated LockHandler thread to handle all lock related operations. When a process
needs to execute a lock/unlock operation, the process places a request in queue. The LockHandler reads the queue and
attempts to insert the appropriate records in to the Lock or LockShared tables. Additionally, the LockHandler will also return
the response to the process that has requested the lock.

The LockHandler will attempt to retry a “wait” lock request every two seconds until the lock attempt succeeds. If a “no-wait”
lock request is specified, the LockHandler will reattempt lock acquisition immediately.

     It is possible that a node may obtain a lock, and then fail to release the lock for several reasons. For example, the node
     could fail, or a problem with the network may prevent communication between the nodes. To prevent other nodes from
     waiting for an unresponsive lock owner, the following heartbeat mechanism has been implemented:
     When a process requests a lock and finds the lock is already held and the heartbeat value has not been updated, it sets
     the “Suspected” flag of the lock record in the database table to 1.
     The lock owner updates the heartbeat and checks the “Suspected” flag of the lock record in the database table every
     60 seconds.
     If the “Suspected” flag is set to 1, the lock owner sets the “Suspected” flag back to 0 and then increases the heartbeat.
     If the lock owner has failed to update the “Suspected” flag and heartbeat, the process that's waiting will periodically
     recheck the “Suspected” flag. After 10 minutes (the default value specified in the deadnodelocktimeout parameter), the
     lock is forcibly removed by deleting the lock record from the database table.

New Parameter

This new locking mechanism implements the deadnodelocktimeout parameter. This parameter specifies the amount of time
that must elapse before a process forcibly removes a lock from the Lock or LockShared table. By default, this parameter is
set to 10, which indicates that 10 minutes must elapse before a record is forcibly removed. 10 minutes is also the minimum
value for this parameter.

This parameter is specified in the sm.ini file. Changing the value of this parameter doesn't require a restart of the server.

1.9.4. Scheduled processes

You can start RAD applications, known as scheduled processes, as unattended background processes. Scheduled processes
are also known as background agents, schedulers, processors, and background tasks. Scheduled processes run at set
intervals and check for specific conditions before executing a RAD application. Each scheduled process has one or more
schedule records that determine the conditions that must be met for the RAD application to run. You can start scheduled
processes from the Scheduler form.

1.9.4.4. Restart stopped background processes automatically

Applies to User Roles: System Administrator
You can use the following two parameters to restart stopped background processes automatically. Note that you must use
these two parameters in conjunction.

     Startup parameter: enableAnubisMonitor: Start Anubis monitor to check the status of the background scheduler thread.
     Startup parameter: anubisPollInterval: Specify the time interval for the Anubis thread to check whether any registered
     scheduler is alive. The default value is 15 and the unit is second.

            Note

           If the background scheduler is killed by either the system status or the operating system's Task Manager, this is
           considered as normal termination and Anubis will not take effect. Anubis will restart the background scheduler
           only when it terminates unexpectedly.

1.9.4.8. Set up background processes with high availability

Service Manager background processes support high availability and multiple Service Manager threads for a scheduled class
can work on multiple servers in parallel. With paralleled background processes, the Service Manager production system
processes the tasks in the scheduled queue more efficiently. In the event of server restart or server failure, the other servers
continue to work on the same class of tasks. For example, two SLA threads are running on background Server 1 and another
two SLA threads are running on background Sever 2. All SLA threads are processing the SLA Task Queue in parallel. If Server
1 is restarting or runs to error, Server 2 continues processing the SLA threads.

Here are some guidelines for your reference when setting up background processes with high availability:
   1. Add a set of backups of the original Service Manager servers that are running background process schedules.
   2. At a minimum, start each background process separately on two Service Manager servers (for example, Server 1 and
     Server 2) by using any methods as follows.
           Run the following command to start all background processes that are defined in the Background Process
           Initialization Registry with the name of startup. Go to System Administration > Ongoing Maintenance > System
           > Startup Information and then search for the startup schedule to view its contents.

                 sm -bg system.start

           Run the following command to start all background schedules that are defined in the Background Processor
           Initialization Registry with a specified name. Go to System Administration > Ongoing Maintenance > System >
           Startup Information to view all available schedules.

                 sm -bg scheduler.start <name of the Background Processor Initialization Registry>

           Run the following command to start a schedule of a specific class.

                 sm -bg scheduler <class of the background process> 60 0 -log:../logs/<class of the
                 background process>.log

   3. On any two servers, use the schedule.monitor scheduler to monitor the background processes.
     When multiple background processes are running in parallel, a schedule record may be locked during processing. If any
     error occurs in the background processes, the record lock can't be cleared and hence becomes invalid. The
     schedule.monitor scheduler can monitor the invalid locks, clear these locks regularly, and send notification emails when
     encountering exceptions.
     To start the schedule.monitor background processes, follow these steps:
        1. (Optional) Customize the email notification conditions by updating the ScheduleCustom Javascript. By default,
           the system sends an email notification to a recipient after completing each of the following actions.
                 Clean up a deadlocked schedule
                 Clean up schedule records which status is running
                 Clean up a schedule that incorrectly stops

This PDF was generated on May 23, 2026  Page 244 of 251
                                                                                    Service Manager 9.81

  In addition, you can perform customizations to the EmailScheduleMonitor email template.
2. Click Ongoing Maintenance > System > Schedule Monitor to open the Schedule Monitor Configuration page.
3. Type or select the following information.

Field                                   Description

                                        email notifications.

                                        Note: This function requires that you have an email

1.9.4.9. Print background process information to log

Sometimes it's uneasy to troubleshoot background processes. Knowing the tasks that Service Manager processes is
important for trace reading. In this case, in addition to debugging with the rtm:3 parameter, you can use the ScheduleInfo
JavaScript to print background process information to log when the scheduler processing a schedule record.
By default, the content of the ScheduleInfo JavaScript may resemble the following.

  var log = getLog("ScheduleInfo");
  function print(scheduleFile){

      log.info("The scheduler begin to run.
  ScheduleName:"+scheduleFile["name"]+",ScheduleID:"+scheduleFile["schedule.id"]);
  }

By using this JavaScript, Service Manager prints the following background process information to the log file.

  $ cat sm.log|grep "The scheduler begin to run"
  1612239(1653063) 06/12/2023 03:36:17.362 JS I ScheduleInfo The scheduler begin to run.
  ScheduleName:Change Notify Sched,ScheduleID:6022090

To include more information, you can update the ScheduleInfo JavaScript by adding more field names from the schedule
table in the database dictionary. For example:

  var log = getLog("ScheduleInfo");
  function print(scheduleFile) {

         var vString=scheduleFile["strings"];
         log.info("The scheduler begin to run. ScheduleName:" + scheduleFile["name"] +
  ",ScheduleID:" + scheduleFile["schedule.id"]+ ", strings: " + vString.getText() );
  }

In this case, the printed background process information may resemble the following.

  1612239(1653061) 06/12/2023 05:19:17.701 JS I ScheduleInfo The scheduler begin to run.
  ScheduleName:message processor record,ScheduleID:6022113, strings: {"1", "email", , "", , ,
  "SOAP-Web", , "C10066"}

1.9.5. Shared memory

Service Manager shared memory is a pool of memory available to all processes on the server. You can control how the server
allocates and manages shared memory using system parameters in the Service Manager initialization file. Allocating too little
shared memory can degrade system performance, and allocating too much wastes system resources.

The shared memory storage report generates a snapshot of shared memory that enables you to monitor usage. If you are
trying to isolate a performance bottleneck, run a report at start-up and periodically throughout the monitoring period. As a
general rule, if Unused falls below 25%, consider increasing the amount of shared memory (see Startup parameters:
shared_memory). If you're not sure how to interpret the shared memory report, contact the customer support.

To run the shared memory report for a Linux or Windows system, issue the following command from a shell prompt (Linux) or
a command prompt (Windows):

  sm -reportshm
